**Question:** How can the adornment of their deeds be attributed to Himself, when it is attributed to Satan in His saying ﴿And Satan made their deeds seem fair to them﴾?

**Answer:** There is a difference between the two attributions. Attributing it to Satan is literal (haqiqah), while attributing it to Allah, Mighty and Majestic, is figurative (majaz). [Mahmud said: "If you ask how the adornment was attributed to His own Self when it was attributed to Satan in His saying ﴿And Satan made their deeds seem fair to them﴾, I say: there is a difference between the two attributions. The attribution to Allah is figurative, and the attribution to Satan is literal. It has been related from al-Hasan that the intended meaning is that He made the works of righteousness seem fair to them, but they were blind to them and did not guide themselves to act upon them."]

Ahmad said: This answer is built upon the corrupt principle that it is obligatory for God to uphold what is best for the servants (al-salah wal-aslah, "what is most beneficial and most optimal"), and that God cannot create for the servant anything except what is beneficial. For this reason he made the attribution of adornment to God figurative and its attribution to Satan literal. Had he reversed the answer, he would have attained the truth. Consider his inclination toward the other interpretation, namely that the intended meaning is works of righteousness, despite its remoteness, because he does not want to undermine his principle. How could that be, when God has built their structure upon its foundations? Moreover, adornment has occurred in a good sense in His saying ﴿But God has endeared faith to you and made it beautiful in your hearts﴾, yet its usage is mostly in other than righteousness, as in His saying ﴿Beautified for people is the love of desires﴾, ﴿The life of this world has been made attractive to those who disbelieve﴾, and ﴿Likewise, [their partners] have made attractive to many of the polytheists﴾. Among what makes it remote to interpret it as works of righteousness is the attribution of the deeds to them in His saying ﴿their deeds﴾, whereas works of righteousness are not attributed to them, because they never did them. The apparent meaning of the attribution indicates this. Do you not see His saying ﴿And faith has not yet entered your hearts﴾ and His saying ﴿Say, "Do not consider your Islam a favor upon me. Rather, God has bestowed favor upon you that He guided you to faith"﴾? So He used the word faith without attributing it to them in both places, because it did not proceed from them, while He attributed outward Islam to them, because it did proceed from them. And God knows best.]

Figurative speech (majaz) has two paths in the science of eloquence (ilm al-bayan). The first is that it belongs to the type called metaphor (isti'arah). The second is that it belongs to the type called attributive figure (majaz hukmi).

As for the first path: when God granted them long life and abundant provision, and they took Allah's favor and kindness toward them as a means to follow their desires, to be arrogant, to prefer this worldly life and ease, and to shun what would require of them difficult obligations and exhausting hardships, then it is as though He made their deeds seem fair to them through that. The angels, may God's blessings be upon them, pointed to this in their saying ﴿But You gave them and their fathers enjoyment until they forgot the remembrance﴾.

The second path: His granting Satan respite and leaving him free until he made their deeds seem fair to them constitutes a clear connection (mulabasah) to the adornment, so it was attributed to Satan, because the attributive figure is validated by some such connections.

It was also said: the intended meaning is the good deeds that they were obligated to perform. Allah made them seem fair to them, but they were blind to them and went astray. This is attributed to al-Hasan. The word "al-'amah" (blindness, confusion) means bewilderment and hesitation, as is the condition of one who has strayed from the path. It is related from one of the Bedouin Arabs that he entered the marketplace and had never seen it before, and he said: "I saw the people (confused, 'amahin)," meaning hesitating in their works and occupations.

﴿Terrible torment﴾ means killing and captivity on the day of Badr. ﴿The greatest losers﴾ means the most extreme in loss, because had they believed, they would have been witnesses over all nations (the martyrs) (shuhada'), so they lost that together with the loss of salvation and God's reward.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 27, verse 6:

"And indeed, you are being given the Qur'an from one who is All-Wise, All-Knowing."

You are receiving the Qur'an and being taught it from (one who is) "any" Wise (Hakim) and "any" Knowing (Alim). This is the meaning of their coming indefinite (nakira). This verse serves as a carpet and preparation for what follows of the narratives (aqasis), and the subtleties of His wisdom and the fine points of His knowledge contained therein.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 27, verse 7:

"Idh" (when) is in the accusative, governed by an implied verb, which is "udhkur" (remember). It is as if he said, following on from that: take from the traces of His wisdom and knowledge the story of Musa. It is also permissible for it to be in the accusative governed by "alim" (knowing). It is related that no one was with Musa, peace be upon him, except his wife, and God referred to her by the word "ahl" (family). Following on from this, the address came in the plural form, which is His saying: "Wait [imkuthu]."

"Al-shihab": the flame. "Al-qabas": the fire that is taken from a flame. He attributed "al-shihab" to "al-qabas" because it may be a qabas and may be other than a qabas.

Whoever reads it with tanwin makes "qabas" a substitute (badal) or a qualifier (sifah), because of the meaning of qabas that it contains. "Al-khabar": the information that one gives about the state of the road, because he had lost his way.

If you ask: "I will bring you news of it" (sa-atikum minha bi-khabar) and "perhaps I will bring you news of it" (la'alli atikum minha bi-khabar) are like two contradictory statements, since one expresses hope and the other certainty. I answer: the one who hopes may, when his hope is strong, say "I will do such-and-such" and "such-and-such will happen," even while allowing for disappointment.

If you ask: how did he use the particle of future "sin" (sa)? I answer: it is a promise to his family that he will bring it to them, even if it is delayed, or because the distance was great.

If you ask: why did he use "aw" (or) and not "wa" (and)? I answer: his hope was based on the idea that if he did not obtain both of his needs, he would not be deprived of one of them: either guidance to the road or the kindling of fire. This was trust in God's custom that He hardly ever combines two deprivations upon His servant. And how could he know, when he said that, that he would succeed in obtaining both of his complete needs from the fire, which are the two honours: the honour of this world and the honour of the Hereafter?

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 27, verse 8:

Anna here is explanatory (mufassira), because the calling (al-nida') in it carries the sense of saying. The meaning is: it was said to him, "Blessed is..." If you ask: could it be the lightened form (mukhaffafa) of the heavy anna, with the pronoun being the pronoun of the matter (damir al-sha'n), and the sense being: he was called out to that "He is blessed..."? I answer: No, because "qad" (indeed) must be present. If you ask: what about assuming it is elided? I answer: That is not valid, because it is a marker that is not elided.

The meaning of ﴿buriká man fi al-nari wa man hawlaha﴾ ("Blessed is whoever is in the fire and whoever is around it") is: blessed is whoever is in the place of the fire and whoever is around its place. Its place is the spot in which it occurred, and that is the blessed spot mentioned in the words of the Exalted: ﴿Called out from the right side of the valley, in the blessed spot﴾ (28:30). This is supported by the reading of Ubayy: "The earth is blessed, and whoever is around it." It is also reported from him: "The fire was blessed, and the one for whom the spot was blessed, and whoever is in it and around it was blessed." The occurrence of a religious matter there is what is meant: namely, God's speaking to Musa, His appointing him as a prophet, and the manifestation of miracles through him. A good thing that occurs in some place spreads its blessing by God to its farthest reaches and disseminates the traces of its blessing to its distant parts; how much more so with such a great matter as occurred in that spot. It was also said: what is meant by "those blessed within it" is Musa and the angels present. Apparently it is general, applying to everyone who was in that land, in that valley, and around them from the land of al-Sham. God has marked the land of al-Sham with blessings in His words: ﴿And We delivered him and Lot to the land which We have blessed for the worlds﴾ (21:71), and it is fitting that it be so. It is the place from which the prophets, upon them be blessings of God, were sent, the place of descent of revelation to them, and the resting place for them, both living and dead. If you ask: what is the significance of God beginning His address to Musa with this when he came? I answer: It is glad tidings to him that a great matter has been decreed, from which blessing will spread throughout all the land of al-Sham. ﴿Glory be to God, Lord of the worlds﴾ is an expression of wonder to Musa, peace be upon him, at this, and a notice that this matter was willed and brought into being by the Lord of the worlds, as an alert that what occurs is of grand matters and great affairs.

The pronoun in "innahu" may be the pronoun of the matter (ḍamīr al-shaʾn), and the matter is: "Anā Allāh" (I am God), as subject and predicate. Al-ʿAzīz al-Ḥakīm (the Mighty, the Wise) are two attributes of the predicate.

It may also refer back to what is indicated by what precedes it, meaning: "The one speaking to you is I, and Allah is an explanation of 'Anā'." Al-ʿAzīz al-Ḥakīm are two attributes of the one explained.

This is a preparation for what He wished to manifest through his hand of miracles. He means: I am the Mighty, the Capable over what is far beyond imagination, such as turning the staff into a snake, the Doer of everything I do with wisdom (ḥikmah) and planning (tadbīr).

If you ask, "What is the clause 'And cast down your staff' coordinated with?" I answer: it is coordinated with "Blessed is whoever is in the fire." The meaning is: he was called, "Blessed is whoever is in the fire," and "that cast down your staff" are both explanations (tafsīr, explanation) of "nādā" (he was called). The meaning is: it was said to him, "Blessed is whoever is in the fire," and it was said to him, "Cast down your staff." The evidence for this is the Exalted's saying, ﴿And that cast down your staff﴾, after His saying, ﴿O Moses, indeed I am Allah﴾, with the explanatory particle "an" repeated, as you say: "I wrote to you that perform the ḥajj and that perform the ʿumrah," or, if you wish, "that perform the ḥajj and ʿumrah."

al-Ḥasan recited "jaʾanna," following the dialect of those who hasten to escape the meeting of two unvocalized letters, so that he says "shaʾabbah" and "daʾabbah." Among these is the recitation of ʿAmr ibn ʿUbayd: "wa-lā al-ḍaʾḍǟlīn." ﴿And did not turn back﴾ means: did not return. It is said: "ʿaqiba al-muqātil" (the fighter turned back) when he charged again after fleeing. He said:

"They did not turn back when it was said, 'Is there any one who will return?'
Nor did they alight at any place on the day of the fierce battle."

[This describes a people as cowardly: when it was said to them, "Is there anyone who will return and go back to the battle?", they did not return to it, nor did they alight at any of its stations on the day of battle; that is, they did not once advance against the enemy. It is also related as "iḏ qīla," meaning "at that time."]

He was frightened only because he thought that this was for a matter directed at him. What confirms this is the saying, ﴿Indeed, the messengers do not fear in My presence﴾. "Illā" here means "but" (lākin), because when the negation of fear was stated absolutely concerning the messengers, that was a likely occasion for doubt to arise, so it was corrected. The meaning is: "But whoever among them has done wrong," that is, a small lapse occurred from him of the kind that is permissible for prophets, like what occurred from Adam, Jonah, David, Solomon, and the brothers of Joseph, and from Moses in striking the Copt. It is likely that this is an allusion to what was found in Moses, and it is one of the allusions whose meaning is subtle. He called it "wrongdoing," as Moses said, ﴿My Lord, I have wronged myself, so forgive me﴾. "Al-ḥasan" and "al-sūʾ": the good is good repentance, and the evil is the ugliness of the sin.

It was also recited: "alā man ẓalama," with the particle of alerting. And from Abū ʿAmr, in the transmission of ʿIṣma: "ḥusnan."

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 27, verse 12:

"In nine signs" is a new (mustaʾnaf) clause, and the preposition (ḥarf al-jarr, the particle that governs a noun in the genitive) in it is attached to an omitted verb (maḥdhūf). The meaning is: go with nine signs to Pharaoh (Fir'awn) and his people, as in the verse:

"I said, 'To the food!' and a group among them said, / 'We envy the humans their food.'" [[The explanation of this line of verse was given in the first part, page 2, so refer to it if you wish. Its corrector (muṣaḥḥiḥuhu) said this.]]

It is also possible that the meaning is: "Throw down your staff and put your hand [into your bosom]: among nine signs," that is, "among the total of nine signs and their count." One might object: the signs were eleven, two of which are the hand and the staff, and the nine are: the splitting (al-Falaq) of the sea, the flood (al-Ṭūfān), the locusts (al-Jarād), the lice (al-Qummal), the frogs (al-Ḍafādiʿ), the blood (al-Dam), the effacing (al-Ṭamsah) of wealth, the drought (al-Jadb) in their deserts, and the shortage (al-Nuqṣān) in their crops.

The commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 27, verse 13:

Al-mubsirah (the clear, evident): it means evident and plain. The seeing is attributed to them (the signs), though in reality it belongs to those who contemplate them, because they were clothed in them (i.e., surrounded by them) and were the cause of seeing them through their sight and reflection upon them. It is also permissible that the literal sense of seeing be taken to refer to every observer of them from among all people of intellect, or that it refer to the seeing of Pharaoh and his chiefs, based on His saying: ﴿and their souls were convinced of them﴾. Or the signs are made as if they could see and thus guide, since the blind cannot be capable of guidance, let alone guide others. From this comes their saying: "a eyeful word" (kalimah 'aynā') and "a blind word" (kalimah 'awrā'), because a good word guides and a bad word misleads. Similar to this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Certainly you know that none sent these down except the Lord of the heavens and the earth as insights (basa'ir)﴾, so He described them as having insight (al-basarah), just as He described them as giving sight (al-ibsar). Ali ibn al-Husayn (may Allah be pleased with them both) and Qatadah recited: mubsirah, which is like: mujbinah (causing cowardice), mubkhilah (causing miserliness), and mujfirah [[His saying "mujfirah": in al-Sihah, "jafara al-fahl 'an al-dirab" means the stallion ceased from mating. From this it is said: fasting is mujfirah, i.e., it cuts off marriage. (A)]], meaning: a place where much seeing (tabassur) occurs.

The waw in "wa-istayqanatha-hā" is the waw of circumstance (wāw al-ḥāl), and a verb (qad) is implied after it. Al-ʿUluww means arrogance and haughtiness toward faith in what Musa brought, as in God's words: ﴿So they were arrogant, and they were a haughty people. They said: "Shall we believe in two mortals like ourselves, while their people are slaves to us?"﴾ It is also read ʿaliyyan and ʿaliyyan (with ḍamma and kasra), just as ʿataiyyan and ʿitiyyan are read.

The purpose of mentioning "the souls" (al-anfus) is that they denied the signs with their tongues while being certain of them in their hearts and inner consciences. Al-istiyqān is more emphatic than al-iyqān. The "clear-seeing" (mubṣira) is set in contrast with the "manifest" (mubīn). What injustice could be more grievous than that of one who believes and is certain that these are clear, evident signs that came from God, and yet obstinately calls them plain, open, undeniable sorcery?

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 27, verse 15:

ʿIlman (knowledge) — a portion of knowledge. [[Mahmud said: "Its meaning is a portion of knowledge." Ahmad (Ibn al-Munayyir) said: indefiniteness here indicates partiality and diminution, and just as indefiniteness may be used to belittle what is indefinite, it may also be used to magnify its status, as has passed just before in His words, ﴿And indeed, you are receiving the Qur'an from One who is Wise and Knowing﴾, where "Wise" and "Knowing" are not preceded by the definite article. The purpose of the indefiniteness is exaltation, as if He had said: "from One who is Wise and Knowing." Thus the apparent sense of His words, ﴿And We gave David and Solomon knowledge﴾, in the context of bestowing favour, is the magnification of the knowledge they were given, as if He had said: "knowledge — what knowledge!" And that is indeed the case, for their knowledge was something great and wondrous, and among it was the knowledge of the speech of birds and of all the other animals, with which God Most High singled them out. Every knowledge, in comparison with the knowledge of God Most High, is small and insignificant. And God knows best.]] Or abundant, copious knowledge.

If you say: Is this not a place for the particle "fa" (then) rather than "waw" (and), as in your saying: "I gave him, and he thanked; I withheld from him, and he was patient"? I say: Yes, but conjoining it with "waw" indicates that what they both said was part of what the granting of knowledge produced in them, and some of its obligations. So that is implied, and then the praise is conjoined to it, as if He had said: "We gave them both knowledge, so they acted upon it, taught it, and recognised the true nature of the blessing in it." [[Mahmud said: "They glorified God's blessing upon them by their saying 'who has favoured us', and they showed humility by their saying 'over many of His believing servants', and did not say 'over His servants', acknowledging that others might excel them, out of caution against arrogance."]] And the favour, and the "many" who were favoured over: those who were not given knowledge, or those who were not given the like of their knowledge.

And in it: they were favoured over many, and many were favoured over them.

In the verse is evidence of the nobility of knowledge, the loftiness of its station, the eminence of its bearers and people, and that the blessing of knowledge is among the greatest blessings. It has magnificent emphasis. Whoever is given it has been given favour over many of God's servants, as He said: ﴿God will raise those who have believed among you, and those who were given knowledge, by degrees﴾. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) named them "the heirs of the prophets," [[Related by Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi, Ibn Majah and Ibn Hibban from the hadith of Abu al-Darda', a hadith which says: "Whoever travels a path seeking knowledge in it..." and in it: "Indeed the scholars are the heirs of the prophets." It has further routes in al-Tabarani. On the subject there are also reports from al-Bara' and Ibn Amr ibn al-As, which Abu Nu'aym related in his book Fadl al-'Alim al-'Afif ʿala al-Jahil al-Sharif. And from Ibn Mas'ud, related by Ibn Hamzah al-Sahmi in Tarikh Jurjan. And from Jabir, related by al-Khatib in Tarikh Baghdad in the biography of Ahmad ibn Muhammad al-Thalji. In its chain is al-Dahhak ibn Hujzah, who is accused of fabricating hadith.]] — only because of their closeness to them in nobility and rank, for they are the upholders of what they were sent to establish.

It also implies that this excellent blessing necessarily entails obligations, among them: that they praise God for what they have been given of favour over others. It also contains a reminder of humility, and that a scholar should believe that although he has been favoured over many, others like them have been favoured over him as well. How fine is the saying of 'Umar: "Everyone is more learned than 'Umar." [[Mentioned earlier in surah al-Nisa'.]]

He inherited from him prophethood and kingship, to the exclusion of his other sons, who numbered nineteen. David was more devoted to worship, and Solomon was more judicious and more thankful for the blessing of God. ﴿And he said: O people﴾, publicizing the blessing of God, exalting it, acknowledging its station, and calling people to believe in the miracle, which is the knowledge of the speech of birds (manṭiq al-ṭayr), and in other great matters he was given. Al-manṭiq (speech) is everything that is vocalized, whether single or compound, meaningful or meaningless.

Yaʿqūb ibn al-Sikkīt titled his book *Iṣlāḥ al-Manṭiq* (The Correction of Speech), and he corrected only single words. The Arabs say: "The dove spoke" (naṭaqat al-ḥamāmah). Every kind of bird understands the sounds of its own kind. What Solomon knew of the speech of birds is what some of them understand from others of their meanings [[The phrase "what some of them understand from others of their meanings" is the wording of al-Nasafi: "al-manṭiq: everything that is vocalized, whether single or compound, meaningful or meaningless, and Solomon, peace be upon him, understood from it as some of it is understood from others." (ʿ)]] and their purposes. It is related that he passed by a nightingale in a tree that was moving its head and tilting its tail, and he said to his companions: "Do you know what it says?" They said: "God and His Prophet know best." He said: "It says:

I have eaten half a date, so let the world be effaced."

A turtledove cried out, and he informed them that it was saying: "Would that these creatures had never been created."

A peacock called out, and he said it was saying: "As you judge, so you will be judged."

A hoopoe called out, and he said it was saying: "Seek forgiveness from God, you sinners."

A ṭīṭawā (a small bird) called out, and he said it was saying: "Every living thing dies, and every new thing wears out."

A swallow called out, and he said it was saying: "Send forward some good, and you will find it."

A ḥadaʾ... a rakhamah (vulture) called out, and he said it was saying: "Glory be to my Lord, the Most High, filling His heaven and His earth."

A dove (qumrī) called out, and he informed them that it was saying: "Glory be to my Lord, the Most High."

He said: The kite (ḥidaʾ) says: "Everything perishes except God." The sandgrouse (quṭāh) says: "Whoever keeps silent is safe." The parrot (babbaghāʾ) says: "Woe to him whose concern is the world." The rooster says:

"Remember God, you heedless ones."

The eagle (nasr) says: "O son of Adam, live as you wish, death will end you." The falcon (ʿuqāb) says:

"In distance from people is intimacy."

The frog says: "Glory be to my Lord, the Holy."

By His words ﴿of everything﴾ he meant the abundance of what was given to him, just as you say: "So-and-so is sought by everyone, and knows everything," meaning that many seek him and turn to him, and that he has abundant knowledge and great store of it. Similar is His words: ﴿and she has been given of everything﴾. ﴿Indeed, this is the manifest bounty﴾ is a statement made in the manner of thanks and praise, as the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "I am the master of the children of Adam, and I say this without boasting" [[Mentioned earlier in the commentary on Surah Yusuf]]. That is, I say this as an expression of thanks, not of pride.

If you ask: how could he say "we were taught" and "we were given," when this is the speech of the arrogant? I answer: there are two possibilities. First, he means himself and his father. Second, this "we" is called the "nūn of the one obeyed" (nūn al-wāḥid al-muṭāʿ, the plural of majesty used by one who is obeyed), and he was an obeyed king. So he addressed those who obeyed him in terms of his own attributes and state. Arrogance is not necessarily part of this. It may be connected to the adornment of kingship, its grandeur, the display of its splendor [[The phrase "the display of its splendor": it is said: its ranks and brilliance. In another copy: its awe, so let it be verified. (ʿ)]] and its governance, which serve public interests, so such display becomes obligatory. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) would do something similar when a delegation came to him, or when he needed to impress an enemy. Do you not see how he commanded al-ʿAbbās, may God be pleased with him, to detain Abū Sufyān until the battalions passed before him? [[Related by al-Bukhārī through the narration of Hishām ibn ʿUrwah from his father in the account of the Conquest: "Abū Sufyān embraced Islam. When [the Prophet] set off, he said to al-ʿAbbās: 'Detain Abū Sufyān at the narrow pass of the mountain until he sees the Muslims.' Al-ʿAbbās detained him, and the battalions began to pass with the Prophet (ﷺ), one battalion after another." It was also related by al-Bayhaqī in al-Dalāʾil through ʿIkrimah from Ibn ʿAbbās, may God be pleased with them both.]]

Narrated that his encampment was a hundred farsakhs by a hundred: twenty-five for the jinn, twenty-five for mankind, twenty-five for the birds, and twenty-five for the wild beasts. He had a thousand tents of glass set upon wooden poles, in which were three hundred wives and seven hundred concubines. The jinn had woven for him a carpet of gold and silk, a farsakh by a farsakh, and his pulpit was set in its middle, made of gold. He would sit upon it, and around him were six hundred thousand chairs of gold and silver: the prophets sat on the golden chairs and the scholars on the silver chairs, and around them were the people, and around the people were the jinn and the devils. The birds shaded him with their wings so that the sun did not fall upon him, and the east wind lifted the carpet and carried it a month's journey. It is also related that he would command the violent wind to carry him and command the gentle breeze to move him. Then God revealed to him while he was travelling between heaven and earth: "I have increased your kingdom: no one speaks a word but the wind casts it into your hearing." It is related that he passed by a plowman and said, "The family of David were given a mighty kingdom," and the wind cast it into his ear. So he descended, walked to the plowman, and said, "I have come to you only so that you do not wish for what you cannot attain," then said, "One single glorification that God accepts is better than what the family of David was given."

﴿فهم يوزعون﴾ means: their first is held back upon their last, i.e., the vanguard of the army is halted until the rear catches up, so that they are gathered together and none of them falls behind, and that is because of the great multitude.

[[The statement "the vanguard of the army" (سلاف العسكر) means its forerunners (متقدموهم). Reported by al-Sihah. (ع)]]

It was said: it is a valley in Syria abounding in ants. If you ask, why did they use ʿalā (on/over) with ataw ("they came")? I answer that it may be understood in two senses. The first is that their coming was from above, so the particle of elevation (ḥarf al-istiʿlāʾ) was used, as Abū al-Ṭayyib said:

*Ah, how far you have exceeded your station as you climbed, and how the stars have drawn near above you.*

Abū al-Ṭayyib al-Mutanabbī said this when a man asked him for praise and he refused. The lām is for emphasis. Shadda is in the passive form, used for exclamation. Its original form was shaddada, like ḥasuna, and the ḍamma of the dāl was moved to the shīn and the letters were assimilated, as is the regular pattern for the exclamative form. The meaning is: how intense is your surpassing of your measure, that is, you have greatly exceeded your due, ascending to a height of elevation that is not yours. He said ʿalayka and not ilayka because the nearness of the stars comes from above, meaning the stars have drawn near to you from on high. The stars may be literal, and then he built the metaphorical ascent upon the physical ascent in order to emphasize the likeness of the first to the second. Or they may be metaphorical for his poetry, which is like the stars in its beauty and in the difficulty of reaching it, in the explicit metaphor form (al-tasrīḥiyya). In this there is a shabah al-tawriya (a suggestion of concealment).

The second sense is that what is meant is crossing the valley and reaching its far end, from the expression atā ʿalā al-shayʾ, meaning he completed it and reached its end. It is as if they wanted to descend at the end of the valley, since as long as the wind carries them through the air, there is no fear of their being crushed.

It was read namlatun, yā ayyuhā l-namlu (﴿O ants﴾), with a ḍamma on the mīm, and also with ḍamma on both the nūn and the mīm. The original form is al-namlu, on the pattern of al-rajul, and the commonly used al-namlu is a lightened form of it, like their saying al-sabʿ for al-sabʿ.

It was said: she used to walk lame, tatakawwas (stumbling and tumbling). In al-Ṣiḥāḥ: kawwasahu ʿalā raʾsihi takwīsan means he turned it over on its head, and kāsa yakūsu means he did that. Kāsa al-baʿīr means the camel walked on three legs, being hobbled. Then she called out, "Yā ayyuhā l-namlu" (﴿O ants﴾), and so on. Solomon heard her speech from three miles away.

It was also said her name was Ṭākhiyya. It is reported from Qatāda that he entered Kufa, and people crowded around him. He said, "Ask me whatever you wish." Abū Ḥanīfa, may God have mercy on him, was present, and he was a young lad. He said, "Ask him about the ant that spoke to Solomon: was it male or female?" They asked him and he was silenced. Abū Ḥanīfa then said, "It was female." He was asked, "How do you know that?" He said, "From the Book of God, His saying ﴿qālat namlatun﴾ (﴿a certain ant said﴾). Had it been male, it would have said qāla namlatun."

Mahmūd (al-Zamakhsharī) said: "When Qatāda entered Kufa, people crowded around him. He said, 'Ask me whatever you wish.' Abū Ḥanīfa, who was young, said, 'Ask him about the ant that spoke to Solomon: was it male or female?' They asked him and he was silenced. Abū Ḥanīfa said, 'It was female.' He was asked, 'How do you know that?' He said, 'Because God, mighty and majestic, said ﴿qālat namlatun﴾, and had it been male He would have said qāla namlatun.'"

Aḥmad (Ibn al-Munayyir) said: I do not know whether to be amazed at him or at Abū Ḥanīfa for having that attributed to him. The ant is like the dove and the sheep: it applies to the male and the female, because it is a generic noun (ism jins). One says namlatun dhakar and namlatun unthā, just as they say ḥamāmatun dhakar and ḥamāmatun unthā, and shāt dhakar and shāt unthā. Its word is feminine, but its meaning allows for it. It may be made feminine because of its form even if it refers to a male. Indeed this is the eloquent and common usage. Do you not see his saying, upon him be blessings and peace (ﷺ): "Do not sacrifice a one-eyed animal, nor a lean one, nor a blind one," how he expressed these attributes in the feminine according to the form of the word, though he did not mean females of livestock only. So God's saying ﴿qālat namlatun﴾ observes the feminine form of the word, while in meaning it is equally open. I have dwelt on this at length, even though no legal ruling depends on it, because he attributed it to the Imam Abū Ḥanīfa, with his insight into the language. Then he made this answer seem marvelous, for Nuʿmān's great knowledge and his insight into transmitted reports. Then he established the matter as it is, preserved for him. How strange, how wondrous! God grants success to what is right.

This is because the ant, like the dove and the sheep, applies to male and female, so the two are distinguished by a marker, as in ḥamāmatun dhakar and ḥamāmatun unthā, and huwa and hiya. It was read: ﴿maskanakum﴾ (﴿your dwellings﴾), and ﴿lā yaḥṭimannakum﴾ (﴿let them not crush you﴾) with the nūn lightened. ﴿Lā yaḥṭimannakum﴾ was also read with a fatḥa and a kasra on the ḥāʾ. Its original form is yaḥtaṭimankum.

Since He made her speak and the ants addressed as if they were rational beings, He gave their address the same treatment as the address of rational beings.

If you ask, what is lā yaḥṭimannakum? I answer: it may be a response to the command, or it may be a prohibition in place of the command. What permitted it to be in place of the command is that it has the sense of: "Do not remain where you are, lest it crush you," as in the idiom lā ʾurayannaka hāhunā ("I do not want to see you here"). He meant: let not the hosts of Solomon crush you. He used the more emphatic form. Similar is the expression: "I marveled at myself and at its compassion (for me)."

The meaning of ﴿فَتَبَسَّمَ ضَاحِكًا﴾ is that he began to laugh, having moved from smiling to laughing. The Prophets, peace be upon them, laughed as well. As for what is related, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) laughed until his molars showed (*nawajidh*), several hadiths are cited for this statement. Among them is the hadith of Ibn Mas'ud: "A man from the Jews came and said: O Muhammad, Allah holds the heavens upon one finger..." The hadith continues: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) laughed until his molars showed." It is agreed upon (*muttafaq 'alayh*). Another is his hadith, traced to the Prophet: "I know the last of the people of the Fire to leave it..." The hadith includes the man's words: "Are you mocking me while you are the King?" and then: "I saw the Prophet (ﷺ) laugh until his molars showed." It is also agreed upon. Another is the hadith of Abu Dharr, may Allah be pleased with him: "A man will be brought forward on the Day of Resurrection, and it will be said: Show him the minor sins..." The hadith continues: "I saw the Prophet (ﷺ)..." until its end. It was related by Muslim. Another is the hadith of Abu Sa'id, traced to the Prophet: "On the Day of Resurrection the earth will be one loaf of bread..." The hadith includes: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) looked at us, then laughed until his molars showed." It is agreed upon. Another is the hadith of Jabir: "Abu Bakr entered while the people were sitting at the door..." and in it Umar said: "If you had seen the daughter of Kharija asking me for maintenance, and I got up and struck her neck." He said: "The Prophet (ﷺ) laughed until his molars showed." It was related by Muslim. Another is the hadith of Ibn Umar, may Allah be pleased with them both: "We were with the Prophet (ﷺ) on a campaign, and the people were struck by hunger..." and in it: "No vessel remained in the army without being filled, and his was left empty. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) laughed until his molars showed." It was related by Ibn Hibban and al-Hakim. Another is the hadith of Salama ibn al-Akwa': "We came to al-Hudaybiyya..." and in it: "I said: O Messenger of Allah, let me choose a hundred men from the people, and I will follow the people and not leave any of them alive except that I kill him. The Prophet (ﷺ) laughed until his molars showed." It is a long hadith, and this wording appears elsewhere in it, related by Muslim. Another is the hadith of Zayd ibn Arqam: "Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, while he was in Yemen, was brought three men who had all had intercourse with one woman in a single purity period..." and in it: "This was mentioned to the Prophet (ﷺ), and he laughed until his molars showed." It was related by Abu Dawud, Ibn Hibban and al-Hakim.

Another is the hadith of Umm Ayman: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) stood at night and urinated into a clay pot. I got up, being thirsty, and drank it without realizing. In the morning he commanded me to pour it out, and I said: I have drunk it. He laughed until his molars showed." It was related by al-Hakim. Another is the hadith of Suhayb concerning eating dates while he had an eye infection. He said: "I eat it from the side of my healthy eye." He said: "The Prophet (ﷺ) laughed until his molars showed." It was related by al-Bazzar in full, and parts of it by Ibn Majah and al-Hakim. Another is the hadith of Ibn Abbas: "Abdullah ibn Rawaha was lying beside his wife. He got up to a slave girl of his and had intercourse with her..." and in it: poetry, and the woman's words: "I believed in Allah and denied my sight." He said: "He went to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in the morning and informed him, and he laughed until his molars showed." It was related by al-Bazzar, and its chain is weak.

The purpose is to emphasize the extent of the Prophet's laughter. Otherwise, the showing of the molars in reality occurs only at great astonishment. Ibn al-Sumayqa' recited it as *dahikan* (ضحكا).

If you ask: what made him laugh in her words? I say: two things. His admiration for what her words indicated of the manifestness of his mercy, the mercy of his armies and their compassion, and the renown of his condition and theirs in the matter of piety; this is her saying ﴿وَهُمْ لَا يَشْعُرُونَ﴾, meaning that if they had perceived, they would not have acted (so). And his joy at what Allah had given him that He had not given to anyone: his hearing what was whispered by some of the *hakkal* (الحكل), a term for what makes no audible sound, a proverb for smallness and paucity (*al-hakkal*, a word for something that makes no sound, used as an image of minuteness and little), and his comprehension of its meaning. For this reason his supplication included asking Allah to inspire him to give thanks for what He had bestowed on him in this respect, and to make him persevere in increasing righteous deeds and piety.

The literal sense of ﴿أَوْزِعْنِي﴾ is: make me retain (*azi'a*) the thanks for Your blessing upon me, hold it fast, restrain it and bind it so that it does not escape from me, until I am never without being grateful to You. He mentioned his parents because a blessing upon a child is a blessing upon the parents, especially a blessing that returns to religion, for if the child is pious, it benefits them through his supplication, his intercession, and the supplication of the believers for them whenever they pray for him and say: May Allah be pleased with you and with your parents.

It is related that the ant sensed the sound of the armies while not knowing that they were in the air, so Solomon commanded the wind to stand still lest they be frightened, until they entered their dwellings. Then he made the supplication. The meaning of ﴿وَأَدْخِلْنِي بِرَحْمَتِكَ فِي عِبَادِكَ الصَّالِحِينَ﴾ is: make me one of the people of Paradise.

**Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 27, verses 20–21:**

"Am" here is the disjunctive (munqati'ah). He looked at the place of the hoopoe and did not see it, so he said: ﴿Why do I not see the hoopoe?﴾, meaning that he did not see it although it was present, perhaps because a cover had concealed it or for some other reason. Then it occurred to him that it was absent, so he turned away from that and began to say: ﴿Or is he among the absent?﴾, as if he were asking about the correctness of what had occurred to him. A similar usage is their saying: "Is it camels or sheep?"

The story of the hoopoe is mentioned as follows: when Sulayman had completed the building of Bayt al-Maqdis, he prepared for the pilgrimage by gathering (the people) [[The commentary's note on "تجهز للحج بحشره": in al-Sihah (a lexicon): "hashartu al-nas ahshuruhum hashran: I gathered the people. From it comes: yawm al-hashr (the Day of Gathering)." (ʿ)]]. He reached the Sacred Precinct and remained there as long as he willed. During his stay he would offer each day five thousand camels, five thousand cows and twenty thousand sheep. Then he resolved to travel to Yemen, so he set out from Makkah in the morning, heading toward Suhayl. He reached Sanʿa' at the time of midday, and that journey was a month's distance. He saw a beautiful land whose greenery pleased him, so he descended to take his midday meal and pray, but they found no water. The hoopoe was his guide [[The commentary's note on "وكان الهدهد قناقنه": al-qanaqin, with a damma, means the guide who leads and the one who knows water in the digging of wells (al-qunan). Al-qunan is the plural of qanah. Al-Sihah gives this in two places. (ʿ)]], and it could see water beneath the ground as one sees water in a glass. The devils would come and strip the earth away as a skin is stripped, and they would extract the water. So he (Sulayman) looked for it because of this. When Sulayman descended, the hoopoe hovered above and saw another hoopoe perched, so it swooped down to it. It described to it the kingdom of Sulayman and everything that had been subjected to him, and its companion mentioned to it the kingdom of Bilqis, and that under her hand were twelve thousand commanders, each commander having a hundred thousand (men). The hoopoe went with it to look, and it did not return until after the afternoon.

It is also reported that a breath of sunlight fell on Sulayman's head, so he looked and found the place of the hoopoe empty. He summoned the chief of the birds, who is the vulture (al-nasr), and asked him about it, but did not find knowledge of it with him. Then he said to the lord of the birds, who is the eagle (al-uqab): "Bring it to me." So it rose up and looked, and then saw it coming, so it made for it. The hoopoe adjured it by God and said: "By the right of Him who empowered you and made you able over me, spare me." So it left it alone, and the hoopoe said: "May your mother be bereaved of you! The Prophet of God has sworn that he will surely punish you." The eagle said: "Did he make an exception?" The hoopoe said: "Yes." The eagle said: "Or he will surely bring me a clear excuse."

When it drew near to Sulayman, it lowered its tail and wings, dragging them over the ground in humility toward him. When it came close to him, he took hold of its head and drew it toward him, and said: "O Prophet of God, remember your standing before the presence of God." Sulayman trembled and pardoned it. Then he questioned it.

As for his punishment (ʿadhab): it was that he should be disciplined with what his condition could bear, so that his fellow kind might take warning from it. It was also said that Sulayman's punishment of the bird was to pluck its feathers and expose it to the sun. It was said that it should be smeared with tar and exposed to the sun. It was said that it should be thrown to the ants to devour it. It was said that it should be placed in a cage. It was said that it should be separated from its companion. It was said that: "I will make you keep company with opposites." It is reported from some of them: "The narrowest of prisons is companionship with opposites." It was said that: "I will make you serve your peers."

If you ask: from where was it lawful for him to punish the hoopoe?

I say: it is permissible that God permit him this, because of the benefit and advantage that he saw in it, just as He permitted the slaughter of livestock and birds for food and for other benefits. And when the birds were subjected to him, and what he had subjected them for could not be accomplished except through discipline and governance, it was permissible for him to be granted what would set things right through it.

The word ﴿ليأتينّي﴾ is also read as ﴿ليأتينني﴾ (with a different emphatic form). Al-sultan means proof and excuse.

If you ask: he swore on one of three things. His oath on one of them is beyond dispute, but how is his oath on the action of the hoopoe valid? And from where did he know that it would bring a sultan, so that he would say: "By God, it will surely bring me a sultan"?

I say: when he joined the three by ﴿أو﴾ (or) within the ruling that is the oath, his statement came to mean: "One of these matters will certainly happen." That is, if the bringing of a sultan were to occur, there would be no punishment or slaughter; and if it did not occur, one of the two would happen. In this there is no claim of knowledge. Moreover, it is permissible that his oath be followed by the two actions upon a revelation from God that it would bring him a clear sultan, so he hedged it with his words ﴿أَوْ لَيَأْتِيَنِّي بِسُلْطَانٍ مُبِينٍ﴾, on the basis of knowledge and certainty.

فَمَكَثَ (*famakatha*, "he stayed"). It is read with the *kaf* vowelled both *fatha* and *damma*. غَيْرَ بَعِيدٍ (*ghayra baʿīd*, "not far"): not a long time, like the phrase "عن قريب" (*ʿan qarīb*, "soon").

God inspired the hoopoe, and it confronted Sulayman with these words, despite the excellence of prophethood, wisdom, numerous sciences and comprehensive knowledge of many things that he had been given. This was a trial for him in his knowledge, and a reminder that among the least and weakest of God's creatures there is one who has encompassed knowledge of what he has not encompassed, so that he would feel small in himself and his knowledge would seem insignificant to him, and it would be a kindness to him in abandoning self-admiration (*iʿjāb*), which is the trial of scholars, and how great a trial it is. To encompass a thing in knowledge means to know it from all its aspects, so that no known matter is hidden from him.

They said: this is evidence against the falsehood of the claim of the Rafidah (a term for the Shiʿa) that the Imam has nothing hidden from him and that no one in his time is more knowledgeable than him.

سبأ (*Sabaʾ*): it is read with *ṣarf* (declension) and without it. It has also been transmitted with the *bāʾ* sukūn. Ibn Kathir, in one transmission, reads "سبا" with an *alif*, as in their saying "ذهبوا أيدي سبا" (they went off in all directions). He is Sabaʾ ibn Yashjub ibn Yaʿrub ibn Qahtan. Whoever makes it the name of the tribe does not decline it; whoever makes it the name of a clan or the great ancestor declines it.

He said:

*From the Sabaʾ of those present at Maʾrib, when*
*they build, beyond its torrent, the great dam.*

[[He praises a man for being from the tribe of Sabaʾ. It was originally the name of Ibn Yashjub ibn Yaʿrub ibn Qahtan, then the tribe was named after him. Maʾrib is their city. It is said it was a palace of their king. It is the object of "الحاضرين" (those present), not declined. "إذ" is a temporal adverb. "من دون" means "in front of". "العرم" is the great dam that holds back the flood from the city.]]

And he said:

*The ones coming to water, and Taym on the heights of Sabaʾ,*
*the hide of buffaloes has bitten their necks.*

[[That is, "الواردون" are they. Taym is the name of a tribe in the highlands of the land of Sabaʾ. By "the hide of buffaloes" is meant the ropes twisted from it, with which captives' necks are bound. Its biting was likened, for the hardness of these ropes, to what can bite, by way of the implicit metaphor (*al-makniyya*). The biting is an imaginative representation (*takhyīl*), and it is valid to borrow it for pinching, by way of the explicit metaphor (*al-tasrīḥiyya*). Sabaʾ, originally, is the epithet of a man from Qahtan whose name was ʿAbd Shams, because he was the first to take captives. He had ten sons. Six went to Yemen: Ḥimyar, Kinda, al-Asad, Ashʿar, Qashʿam and Bajīla. Four went to Syria: Lakhm, Judhām, ʿĀmila and Ghassān. Their well-known tribes were named after them.]]

Then the city of Maʾrib was named Sabaʾ, and between it and Sanʿāʾ is a three-day journey. Likewise Maʿāfir was named after Maʿāfir ibn Add. It may be intended to mean both the city and the people.

النبأ (*al-naba'*, "the news") is information of significance. His saying "مِنْ سَبَإٍ بِنَبَإٍ" (*min Sabaʾin bi-naba'in*, "from Sabaʾ with news") is of the kind of speech that the scholars of rhetoric call *al-badīʿ* (rhetorical ornamentation), which is among the fine points of speech related to wording, on condition that it comes naturally, or that it is crafted by someone who knows the essence of speech, preserving with it the soundness and correctness of the meaning. Here it has come beyond soundness and is therefore excellent, novel in wording and meaning. Do you not see that if "بنبإ" were replaced with "بخبر" (*bi-khabar*), the meaning would still be sound, but as it came is more sound, because of the additional sense in *naba'*, which fits the description of the situation.

The woman was Balqis, daughter of Sharahil. Her father was king of the whole land of Yemen. Forty kings had preceded him, and he had no child other than her, so she gained control of the kingdom. She and her people were Magians who worshipped the sun.

The pronoun in ﴿تَمْلِكُهُمْ﴾ (they rule over) refers to Saba'. If by it is meant the people, the matter is clear. If the city is meant, the meaning is that she rules its inhabitants.

It has been said in describing her throne that it was eighty cubits long by eighty wide and eighty high. It has also been said that the figure was thirty instead of eighty. It was made of gold and silver, adorned with various kinds of jewels, its legs were of red and green ruby, pearls and emerald, and upon it were seven chambers, each chamber with a locked door.

If you ask: how did the hoopoe regard her throne as great when he had seen the kingdom of Sulayman? I answer: it is possible that her station is judged small in comparison with the station of Sulayman, so that the throne appeared great to him on her behalf. It is also possible that Sulayman had no throne like it, even though his kingdom was great in every respect, just as some governors of the outlying regions may possess something that the king who rules over them and employs them does not possess.

As for the storytellers (al-qussas) who stop at His words ﴿وَلَهَا عَرْشٌ﴾ (she has a mighty throne) and then begin with ﴿عَظِيمٌ وَجَدْتُها﴾ (mighty; I found her), intending "a great matter: that I found her and her people prostrating to the sun", they are of the foolish (nawka, plural of anwak, meaning stupid). In trying to avoid the hoopoe's regarding her throne as great, they fell into a grave error, which is a distortion of the Book of God.

If you ask: how did she say ﴿وَأُوتِيَتْ مِنْ كُلِّ شَيْءٍ﴾ (she has been given of everything), when Sulayman said ﴿وَأُوتِينا مِنْ كُلِّ شَيْءٍ﴾ (we have been given of everything), as if he had made the two equal? I answer: there is a clear difference between them, because Sulayman, peace be upon him, attached his words to what was a miracle from God, namely the teaching of the speech of birds. He first referred to what had been given him of prophethood, wisdom and the means of religion, and then to kingship and the means of worldly life. The hoopoe, however, attached his words to kingship and meant only what she had been given of the worldly means appropriate to her condition. So there is a vast distance between the two statements.

If you ask: how was her location hidden from Sulayman, when the distance between his encampment and her city was near, a three-day journey between Sana'a and Ma'rib? I answer: perhaps God, may He be exalted, concealed that from him for a benefit He saw, just as He concealed the whereabouts of Yusuf from Ya'qub.

**Question:** From where did the hoopoe (al-hudhud) get the guidance to know God, that prostration to Him is obligatory, to deny their prostration to the sun, to attribute it to Satan, and to have it adorned for them?

**Answer:** It is not far-fetched that God inspired him with that, just as He inspired birds and the rest of the animals with subtle knowledge that sound-minded, intelligent people barely arrive at. Whoever wishes to investigate this should consult the *Book of Animals* (Kitab al-Hayawan), especially since this was the time of a Prophet to whom the birds were subjected, whose speech (manțiq) was taught to him, and this was made a miracle for him.

Whoever reads it with the shadda (intensive form, *saddahum*) means: "He barred them from the way, so that they would not prostrate," so the preposition is elided before *an* (that). It is also permissible that *la* is an added particle (zā'ida), and the meaning would be: "They are not guided to prostrate." Whoever reads it with the light form (*alla yasjudu*), then *alla* is "*an* + *la*" (that they not prostrate). *Alā* is an interjection calling attention, *yā* is the vocative particle, and what it addresses is omitted, as in the verse of the one who said:

*Alā yā asliminī yā dāra Mayy 'alal-balā*
*Wa lā zāla munhalan bi-jar'ā'ika al-qaṭr*

(This is Dhu al-Rummah's line.) *Alā* here is an opening particle of attention, so *yā* has no meaning but calling, and the one called is omitted; its estimate is: "O house of Mayy, be safe," and he dispensed with it by what follows it, omitting it out of concern for seeking safety for her. In repeating her call there is a kind of lamentation. *Mayy* is a truncated form of *Mayya*.

The truncation of the *mudāf ilayhi* (the genitive complement) is a poetic necessity, which the preceding vocative made good. *'Alā* is in the sense of *ma'a* (with), meaning: "Be safe even if you are worn out, for if the house does not remain, the traces will suffice for me." *Munhalan* means poured out (as in rain). *Al-jar'ā'* is the feminine of *al-ajra'*, which is a place whose soil is mixed with pebbles. *Al-qaṭr* is rain; he prays for fertility for her.

In the reading of Ibn Mas'ud, and it is the reading of al-A'mash, there is *hallā* (instead of *alā*), and *hallā* results from changing the two hamzas into *hā'*. From Ibn Mas'ud also: *halā tasjudūn*, meaning *alā tasjudūn* (in the second person address). In the reading of Ubayy: "Will you not prostrate to God, who brings forth the hidden thing (al-khabʾ) in the heavens and the earth, and knows what you conceal and what you disclose?" The hidden thing is named by its verbal noun: it is plants, rain, and other things which He, Mighty and Exalted, has hidden among His unseen things.

It is also read *al-khabb* (with the hamza eased by deletion), and *al-khabā* (with the hamza eased by conversion), which is the reading of Ibn Mas'ud and Malik ibn Dinar. Its justification is that it is derived according to the dialect of those who say at pause: *hādhā al-khabū*, *ra'aytu al-khabā*, *wa marartu bil-khabā*, and then they apply the continuous speech (*waṣl*) to the pause form, not according to the dialect of those who say *al-kam'a* and *al-ḥam'a*, because that is weak and despised. It is also read *yakhfūna* and *yu'linūna* with *yā'* and with *tā'*.

It is said that "From *aḥaṭtu* to *al-ʿaẓīm*" is the speech of the hoopoe. It is said that it is the speech of the Lord of Glory.¹ In the bringing forth of the hidden thing there is a sign that it is from the speech of the hoopoe, because of his engineering skill and his knowledge of water beneath the earth; and this is by inspiration from Him who brings forth the hidden thing in the heavens and the earth, exalted be His power and subtle His knowledge. The keen-eyed person of insight, illumined by the light of God, cannot fail to recognize, by his bearing, speech and characteristics, the marks of everyone specialized in a craft or a branch of knowledge. **Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 27, verse 40:**

﴿The one who had knowledge of the Scripture﴾: a man who had the Greatest Name of Allah (*ism Allah al-a'zam*, the name by which He is supplicated most effectively), which is "Ya Hayy, Ya Qayyum" (O Living, O Self-Subsisting). It is also said: "Ya Ilahana wa Ilaha kulli shay'in, ilahan wahidan, la ilaha illa Anta" (O our God and God of everything, one God, there is no god but You). It is also said: "Ya Dhal-Jalali wal-Ikram" (O Possessor of Majesty and Honor). Al-Hasan, may Allah be pleased with him, reported: "Allah" and "al-Rahman."

It is also said that he was Asif ibn Barkhiya, the scribe of Sulayman, peace be upon him, and he was a truthful man of knowledge. It is also said: his name was Ustum. It is also said: he was Jibril. It is also said: he was an angel whom Allah strengthened Sulayman with.

It is also said: he was Sulayman himself, as if he found the 'Ifrit slow, so he said to him: "I will show you what is faster than what you say."

From Ibn Lahi'a: "It has reached me that he was al-Khidr, peace be upon him."

﴿Knowledge of the Scripture﴾: that is, the revealed Scripture, which is the knowledge of revelation and the laws (*shara'i*). It is also said: it is the Preserved Tablet (*al-Lawh*). And "the one who had knowledge of it" was Jibril, peace be upon him.

﴿Before your gaze returns to you﴾ (*ata-ka*, in both places): it may be a verb and an active participle. *Al-tarf* is the movement of your eyelids when you look, so it is used in place of looking. Since the one who looks is described as sending out the gaze, as in the saying of the poet:

*"And when you sent out your gaze as a scout*
*for your heart one day, the sights wearied you.*
*You saw what you cannot possess all of,*
*nor can you be patient with part of it."*

This is by a Bedouin woman, whom a Bedouin man looked at, and he addressed her with poetry asking about her circumstances and her beauty, as if he were seeking to seduce her. She replied to him in this way. It is also said: it belongs to a poet of the *Hamasa*.

The sending out of the sight toward beautiful sights is likened to sending out a scout ahead of a caravan to find a place of fertile pasture, in the form of a *tasrihiyya* (a metaphor in which the comparison is made explicit by naming the thing compared). "Scout" (*ra'idan*) is a *tarshih* (a complementary word that supports the metaphor), because it suits the sending out. "One day" (*yawman*) is an adverb modifying it. "The sights" (*al-manathir*) are the points of looking. He cited their wearying him by his saying: "You saw what you cannot possess all of, nor can you be patient with part of it." So his eye was the cause of his heart falling into the bewilderment of passion and the burning of longing.

The verse describes the gaze as being returned, and it describes the gaze as turning back. The meaning of His saying ﴿before your gaze returns to you﴾ is that you send your gaze toward something, and before you return it, you see the throne before you. It is reported that Asif said to Sulayman, peace be upon him: "Extend your eyes until your gaze reaches its limit." So he extended his eyes and looked toward Yemen. Asif called upon Allah, and the throne was made to sink into its place in Ma'rib. Then it appeared (*nabagha*; in *al-Sihah* [the lexicon], "nabagha al-shay'" means it appeared) before the assembly of Sulayman, peace be upon him, in al-Sham, by the power of Allah, before his gaze returned.

It is also permissible that this be an illustration of how short the time of bringing it was, as you say to your companion: "Do such-and-such in a moment," "in the blink of an eye," "turn and you will see me," and similar things, meaning speed.

﴿Whoever gives thanks, gives thanks only for himself﴾: because thanks lifts from him the burden of obligation, protects him from the mark of ingratitude, binds the blessing to him, and draws more of it.

It is also said: thanks is a bond for existing blessings and a snare for lost blessings. In the words of some of the earlier scholars: "The ingratitude for blessings is ruin, and rarely does a fleeing she-camel stay in her place and return. So summon what has run away with thanks, and keep what remains with generous hospitality." Know that the complete covering of Allah's concealment will soon be diminished if you do not hope to have reverence for Allah.

﴿My Lord is Self-Sufficient, Generous﴾: He is free of need of thanks, and generous in bestowing favors upon the one who is ungrateful for His blessing. What Sulayman, peace be upon him, said when seeing the throne, giving thanks to his Lord, followed the custom of his fellow prophets of Allah and the sincere servants among His worshippers, who receive the coming blessing with good thanks, just as they bear the deposited blessing with beautiful patience.

﴿نَكِّرُوا﴾ (Nakkiru, "disguise it"): make it unrecognisable, altered from its form and shape, as a man disguises himself from people so that they will not recognise him.

They said: "Make its front its back, and its top its bottom." It is also read as ﴿ننظر﴾ (nanzur, "we will see"), with the verb in the jussive (jazm, the mood after a conditional answer) and, with the verb in the indicative (raf', the nominative), as a resumed sentence (istinaf, a new clause). The meaning is: ﴿أَتَهْتَدِي﴾ (ataHtadi, "will she be guided?") to recognising it, or to the correct answer when she is asked about it, or to the religion and faith in the prophethood of Sulayman (peace be upon him), when she sees that clear miracle: how it came before her, though she had left it behind and had locked the doors upon it and posted guards over it.

Here are three words: the particle of alerting, the particle of comparison (kaf al-tashbih), and the demonstrative. He did not say, "Is this your throne?" but rather, "Is it like this, your throne?" so that it would not be a prompting (talqin) of the answer. Therefore she turned to the expression mentioned in the recitation, to match her state, and God knows best. Al-Sarh: the palace. It is also said to mean the courtyard of the house. Ibn Kathir read *sa-aqīhā* with a hamza. Its basis is that he heard *su'uqan*, and so he treated it as singular. *Mumarrad* means smooth.

It is related that before the Queen of Sheba's arrival, Sulayman (peace be upon him) ordered a palace of white glass built on her route, with water flowing beneath it, and fish and other sea creatures placed in it. He set his throne at its entrance and sat upon it, while the birds, the jinn and mankind gathered around him. He did this to increase her awe of his authority, to confirm his prophethood, and to strengthen her in the religion. It is claimed that the jinn disliked the idea of his marrying her, because she would disclose their secrets to him, since she was the daughter of a jinn woman. It is also said that they feared he might have a son by her who would combine the cunning of the jinn and of mankind, and that the kingdom would then pass from Sulayman to a worse and more fearsome power. So they told him: "There is something wrong with her intellect. She has hair on her shins, and her foot is like a donkey's hoof." He therefore tested her intellect by disguising the throne, and he built the palace so that he could see her shins and feet. When she uncovered them, they were the most beautiful of people's shins and feet, and she was not hairy. Then he turned his gaze away and called to her: ﴿It is a palace smoothed of glass﴾.

It is also said that she was the reason for the making of al-nurah (depilatory). He ordered the devils to make it, and they did. Sulayman married her, loved her, confirmed her in her kingdom, and ordered the jinn to build for her Saylahin and Ghumdan. [[His words "they built for her Saylahin and Ghumdan": In al-Sihah, "Saylahun" is a town. In the section on "naṣb," it says that the Arabs, in Nusaybin and similar names, Filastin, Saylahin, Basimin and Qinnasrin, have two usages: first, to keep the ya' and treat it as a diptote; and second, to inflect the sound plural with ya' and nun in the accusative and genitive, and with waw and nun in the nominative. In the section on "ghamada," it says: Ghumdan is a palace in Yemen. In the section on "sana'a," al-masani' means the fortresses. (ʿ)]] He would visit her once a month and stay with her for three days, and she bore him a child. It is also said that he instead married her to Dhu Tubba', king of Hamdan, and gave him authority over Yemen, and ordered Zawba'a, the chief of the jinn of Yemen, to obey him. He built the fortresses for him, and he remained in power until Sulayman died. ﴿I have wronged myself﴾.

She means by her disbelief in what came before. It is also said that she thought Sulayman would drown her in the deep water, so she said: "I have wronged myself through my bad opinion of Sulayman (peace be upon him)."

Also read: "an uʿbudū" with a damma on the bāʾ (following the nūn), [meaning "that worship [Allah]"]: "they are two parties, a believing party and a disbelieving party."

It was also said: the two parties intended are Ṣāliḥ (peace be upon him) and his people, before any of them had believed. They dispute (yakhtaṣimūn): each party says, "The truth is with me."

Al-sayyiʾah: the punishment; al-ḥasanah: repentance. If you ask: what is the meaning of their seeking to hasten the punishment before the good (repentance)? That would only be the case if both were expected, one before the other. I say: out of their ignorance, they used to say, "If the punishment that Ṣāliḥ (peace be upon him) threatens does come, as he claims, then we will repent and seek forgiveness at that time," supposing that repentance is accepted at that moment. But if it does not come, then we remain as we are. So Ṣāliḥ (peace be upon him) addressed them according to their own saying and belief. Then he said to them: ﴿Why do you not seek forgiveness from Allah before the punishment descends?﴾ ﴿That perhaps you may be shown mercy.﴾ This is a warning to them about the error in what they said, and a rebuke for their ignorance in what they believed.

The man would set out on a journey and pass a bird and drive it away (yazjuruhu). If it passed on his right (sanih), he took it as a good omen (tayammun); if it passed on his left (barih), he took it as a bad omen (tashaum). [[His saying "if it passes on the right (sanih), he takes it as a good omen..." etc. The sanih is that which passes on your right side, of a gazelle, bird or other, by passing from your left to your right. The barih is that which passes on your left, by passing from your right to your left, as stated in al-Sihah. (Gh.)]]

When they attributed good and evil to the bird, the expression was extended (ista'ir) to that which was the cause of them, namely the decree and apportionment of God, or the deeds of the servant, which are the cause of mercy and retribution. From this they said: "The bird is God's, not your bird," meaning: the dominant decree of God, to which good and evil are ascribed, not your bird by which you take omens of good and ill.

When they said, "We take omen from you" ( itayarna bikum), meaning: we consider you a bad omen, and they had suffered drought, He said: ﴿Your omen is with God﴾, meaning your cause from which your good and evil come is with God, namely His decree and apportionment; if He wills, He provides for you, and if He wills, He deprives you. It is also permissible that it means: your deeds are recorded with God, and from them there befell you what befell you, as a punishment and a trial. From this is His saying: ﴿Your omen is with you﴾ and ﴿And every person We have fastened his omen to his neck﴾. It was also read tatayyarna bikum, according to the original form. The meaning of tatayyara bihi is: he took it as a bad omen; and tatayyara minhu: he shrank from it.

﴿You are being tried﴾: you are being tested, or you are being punished, or Satan tempts you with his whispering the omen (al-tiyara).

...the city, al-Hijr. The specifier of nine is given as *rahṭ* (a group of men) because it carries the sense of a group, so it is as if it were said: nine persons. The difference between *rahṭ* and *nafar* (a small company): *rahṭ* is from three to ten, or from seven to ten.

*Nafar* is from three to nine. Their names, according to Wahb, are: al-Hudhayl ibn Abd Rabb; Ghanm ibn Ghanm; Rabab ibn Mihraj; Mudda' ibn Mihraj; Umayr ibn Kardaba; Asim ibn Makhrama; Subayt ibn Sadaqa; Sum'an ibn Saffa.

Qidar ibn Salif: they are the ones who undertook to hamstring the she-camel. They were the arrogant ones of the people of Salih, peace be upon him, and they were from the sons of their nobles. ﴿And who do not reform﴾ means that their affair is pure corruption, unmixed with any good, unlike some corrupters in whom a little good may occasionally appear. ﴿They said, swearing one to another﴾: *taqāsamū* may be an imperative or a report, in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) with *qad* understood, meaning: they said, while swearing to one another. It was also read *tuqāsimū*. It was read *latubayyitannahu*, with *ta*, *ya* and *nun*. With *nun* and *ta*, *taqāsamū* admits both possibilities. With *ya*, it is only admissible as a report.

*Al-taqāsum* and *al-taqsum* are like *al-tazāhur* and *al-tazahhur*: a mutual oath. *Al-bayāt* is surprising the enemy by night. It is related of Alexander that he was advised to make a night attack, and he said: "It is not among the ceremonial dignities of kings to steal victory." It was read *mahlika*, with *mīm* and *lām* fatḥa or kasra, from *halaka*; and *mahlika* with *mīm* ḍamma, from *ahlaka*. It may be a verbal noun, a time, or a place.

If you ask: how could they be truthful when they denied what they had done, having brought a report contrary to what was reported?

Answer: It seems they believed that if they made a night attack on Salih and also on his family, and combined the two raids, not one of them only, and then said "we did not witness the destruction of his family," mentioning only one of them, they would be truthful, since they had carried out both raids and not just one. This is clear proof that lying is ugly in the eyes of the unbelievers who do not know the Sharia and its prohibitions, and it does not occur to them. Do you not see that they intended to kill the Prophet of God, yet did not consent to be liars, until they devised for truthfulness a stratagem by which they could escape from lying?

[Ahmad said: The stratagem of al-Zamakhshari for establishing the rule of good and evil by reason is closer than their stratagem, which God Most High called a plot, because his purpose in paving the way for their stratagem is to cite, in support of the aforementioned rule, the agreement of the people of Lot with it, since they found lying repugnant by their intellects, not by the Sharia. How can this be completed for him or for them, when they are plainly lying in their saying "we did not witness the destruction of his family"? For they did both acts, and whoever does both and then denies one of them has not escaped doubt in his lie. The stratagem would have been complete only if they had done one act and been accused of doing two, and then denied the whole. For this reason the scholars did not differ that whoever swears "I will not strike Zayd," then strikes Zayd and Amr, has broken his oath; unlike one who swears "I will not strike Zayd and Amr," then strikes Amr alone; or "I will not eat two loaves," then eats one of them; for such a case is a matter of scholarly disagreement regarding whether it is a breach. Since it is established that these people are plainly lying in their saying "we did not witness the destruction of his family," and that they have no stratagem to escape from lying, then their affair is either that they are rational, in which case they would not agree upon believing in truthfulness through this stratagem while certain it is not a stratagem, and their denial is not close to truth; or the argument of al-Zamakhshari for establishing his religious rule on his claim falls, since the rule of good and evil by reason is one of the foundations of the creed of the Qadariyya, through the agreement of people who are not rational upon its soundness. Let him be content with what he has accepted for his religion. And peace.]

Their plot: what they concealed of planning to destroy Salih, peace be upon him, and his family. God's plot: destroying them from where they did not perceive; it is likened to the plot of the schemer, by way of metaphor. It is related that Salih had a mosque in al-Hijr, in a ravine, where he would pray. They said: "Salih claims that he will be destroyed by us within three days. We will destroy him and his family before the three days." So they went out to the ravine and said: "When he comes to pray, we will kill him, then return to his family and kill them." God sent a rock from the mountainside, *hayālahum* (opposite them), in a continuous rain, one drop after another; and *qa'ada hiyālahu* means "sat opposite him." Let him be content with what he has accepted for his religion. And peace.]

Their plot: what they concealed of planning to destroy Salih, peace be upon him, and his family. God's plot: destroying them from where they did not perceive; it is likened to the plot of the schemer, by way of metaphor. It is related that Salih had a mosque in al-Hijr, in a ravine, where he would pray. They said: "Salih claims that he will be destroyed by us within three days. We will destroy him and his family before the three days." So they went out to the ravine and said: "When he comes to pray, we will kill him, then return to his family and kill them." God sent a rock from the mountainside, *hayālahum* (opposite them), in a continuous rain, one drop after another; and *qa'ada hiyālahu* means "sat opposite him." Its root is *wāw*, as the *Ṣiḥāḥ* states. They hurried, and the rock closed over the mouth of the ravine upon them. Their people did not know where they were, nor did they know what had happened to their people; God punished each of them in his place, and saved Salih and those with him. It was also said: they came at night with their swords drawn, and God sent angels to fill the house of Salih, and they struck them with stones: they saw the stones but did not see the one throwing them.

﴿That We destroyed them﴾ is a resumption (isti'nāf). Whoever reads it with *fatḥa* makes it a substitute for *al-'āqiba* (the outcome), or the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: it is their destruction; or puts it in the accusative in the sense of "because we"; or as the predicate of *kāna*, meaning: the outcome of their plot was destruction. ﴿Empty﴾ is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) in which what is indicated by that operates. 'Isa ibn Umar read *khāwiyatun* with *ḍamma*, as the predicate of the omitted subject.

And mention Lot; or [read it as] "We sent Lot," as an indication of "And We certainly sent" (*wa-laqad arsalna*) in the verse. *Idh* (إذ) is a substitution (*badal*) for the first [i.e., for *Lot*], and an adverbial of time (*zarf*) for the second. "And you are looking on" (﴿وَأَنْتُمْ تُبْصِرُونَ﴾) is from the sight of the heart, meaning: you know that it is an abomination that you were not the first to commit, and that God created the female only for the male, and did not create the male for the male, nor the female for the female. So it opposes God in His wisdom and His judgement, and your knowledge of this makes your sins greater and more deeply ugly and abhorrent. In this is evidence that the ugly act is uglier when it comes from God than when it comes from His servants, because He is the most knowing of those who know and the most wise of those who judge. Or [it means]: you see it, some of you from others, because they used to commit it openly in their assemblies, not concealing it from one another out of licentiousness and debauchery, and as a sign of their open disobedience. It seems Abu Nuwas built his poem on their doctrine when he said:

*Speak out the name of what you do, and leave me with allusions,*
*for there is no good in pleasures without concealment.*

*[Ala fasqini khamran wa qul li hiya al-khamr*
*wa la tasqini sirran idha amkana al-jahr]*

*[Speak out the name of whom you desire, and leave me with allusions,*
*for there is no good in pleasures without concealment.]*

These are by Abu Nuwas. *Ala* (ألا) is an opening particle for alerting attention, so it is as if he said: "Attention! Pour me [wine]." "And say to me, it is the wine": that is, openly name it. His words "when disclosure is possible" are a caution. *Baha al-shay'* means it appeared; *baha bihi* means he made it appear, i.e., reveal the name of the one you love as you reveal the name of wine. It is also transmitted as *wabih bi-ism ma ta'ti*, that is, "what you do." *Da'ni* (دعني) means "leave me," and it implies the meaning of "keep me away," so it takes *min*. It is a metaphor for prohibiting the mention of allusions (*kuna*, the plural of *kunya*), which is what indicates a thing by a hidden indication. The hidden expression is likened explicitly to a veiling screen.

Or [it means]: you see the traces of the disobedient ones before you and what befell them. If you say: you have explained *tubsirun* as "knowledge," and after it [the verse says] "Nay, you are a people who are ignorant" (﴿بَلْ أَنْتُمْ قَوْمٌ تَجْهَلُونَ﴾), how can they be both knowledgeable and ignorant? I say: he means that you act like the ignorant in [committing] what is an abomination while you know it, or that you are ignorant of the consequence. Or he means by ignorance the foolishness and debauchery in which they were. If you say: *tajhaluna* is an attribute of *qawm* (a people), and the qualified noun has a third-person form, so why not make the attribute agree with the qualified noun and read it with *ya'* rather than *ta'*? And likewise "Nay, you are a people who are being tested" (﴿بَلْ أَنْتُمْ قَوْمٌ تُفْتَنُونَ﴾)? I say: the third person and second person were combined, and the second person was given precedence, because it is stronger and more firmly rooted than the third person.
