He (ﷺ) was commanded to recite these verses, which give clear proofs of God's oneness, His power over everything, and His wisdom, and to begin by praising God and sending peace upon His prophets and the chosen among His servants. In this there is excellent instruction and a directive to good manners. It encourages seeking blessing and benefit through these two forms of remembrance, and draws on their status to help the listener accept what is conveyed and pay attention to it, so that it settles in their hearts in the place the speaker desires. Scholars, preachers and admonishers have inherited this practice from generation to generation: they praise God, the Mighty and Majestic, and send blessings upon the Messenger of God (ﷺ) before every beneficial lesson, before every admonition and reminder, and at the start of every sermon. Those who write formal correspondence followed them, beginning their letters on conquests, congratulations and other significant events with this formula. It has been said: the verse is connected to what precedes it, and it commands praise of God for the destruction of the disbelieving nations, and blessings upon the prophets, peace be upon them, and their followers who were saved. It has also been said: it is addressed to Lot, peace be upon him, that he should praise God for the destruction of his people's disbelievers, and greet the one whom God chose, saved from their destruction, and protected from their sins.

It is known that there is no good at all in what they associate with God, such that one would weigh it against the One who is the creator and owner of all good. Rather, this is a way of confronting them and rebuking them. [[Mahmud (al-Zamakhshari) said: "It is known that there is no good in what they associate with Him, such that it would be weighed against the One who is the creator and owner of all good. Rather, it is a way of confronting them and rebuking them." Ahmad (Ibn al-Munayyir) said: "This is a statement that is accepted, after you replace his words 'the creator of all good' with 'the creator of every thing' (khaliq kulli shay'), for the phrase 'the creator of all good' (khaliq kulli khayr) is a specification by decree, or a hidden association. The clear monotheism is what we have stated. And God, glorified and exalted, knows best."]] It is also a mockery of their state. They preferred the worship of idols over the worship of God, yet no sensible person prefers one thing over another except for a reason that moves him to prefer it, such as an increase in good or benefit. So they are told, while it is known that there is no good in what they preferred, and that they did not prefer it for any increase in good but out of desire and frivolity, in order to alert them to their extreme error, their deep ignorance, their corruption of discernment, and their rejection of reason, and so that they may know that preference must be for a greater good. A similar case is what He relates about Pharaoh: ﴿Or am I not better than this one who is contemptible?﴾, although he knew that Moses had nothing like his rivers that flowed beneath him.

Then God, glorified be He, enumerated the goods and benefits, which are the effects of His mercy and bounty, as He enumerated them in another place, and then said: ﴿Is there any of your associates who does any of that?﴾

It is read as yushrikun with the letter ya' and also with the letter ta'.

It is reported from the Messenger of God (ﷺ) that when he recited it, he would say: "Rather, God is better and more lasting, more glorious and more noble." [[This was mentioned by al-Tha'labi without a chain of narration. Al-Bayhaqi recorded it in Shu'ab al-Iman in the ninth chapter, from the narration of Jabir al-Ju'fi, from Abu Ja'far, who said: "Ali ibn al-Husayn used to mention that the Prophet (ﷺ), when he finished the Qur'an, — and he mentioned a long hadith — and in it: 'And praise be to God, and peace upon His servants whom He has chosen. ﴿Is God best, or what they associate?﴾ Rather, God is better, more lasting, more noble, and greater than what they associate.'"]]

**Question:** What is the difference between the two instances of *am* (أم) in ﴿Or [is what] they associate [better]?﴾ and ﴿Or [is He Who] created the heavens and the earth [better]?﴾

**Answer:** The first is *muttasila* (connected, *ittisal*), because the meaning is: "Which of the two is better?" The second is *munqati'a* (disconnected), with the meaning of *bal* (rather) and the interrogative *hamza*, because God, exalted is He, said: ﴿Is God better, or what they associate?﴾ Then He said, as if rejecting this: ﴿Rather, [is] He Who created the heavens and the earth better?﴾ This is a reproach to them, establishing that whoever is able to create the world is better than a lifeless object that is unable to do anything.

Al-A'mash read *amman* (أمن) with a light (*takhfif*) pronunciation. Its explanation is that it is taken as a substitute (*badal*) for *Allah*, as if He had said: "Is He Who created the heavens and the earth better, or what you associate?"

**Question:** What is the point in shifting the report from the third person (*ghayba*) to the first person of speech (*takallum*), about His own Essence, in His saying ﴿and We caused to grow﴾?

**Answer:** It emphasizes the meaning that the act is specific to His Essence, and it signals that causing gardens of different kinds, colours, tastes, scents and shapes to grow, with their beauty and delight, from one water, is something that none can do except Him alone. Do you not see how He hinted at the meaning of exclusivity with His saying ﴿You could not have caused their trees to grow﴾? The meaning of *al-kaynuna* (existence, *kawn*) is *al-inbighaʾ* (being fitting or possible). He intended that such a thing is impossible from anyone other than Him. Likewise His saying ﴿Rather, they are﴾ after the address (*khitab*) is more forceful in refuting their opinion.

*Al-hadiqa* (garden) is an orchard enclosed by a wall, from *al-ihdaq* (encircling), which is surrounding. It is said that *dhāt* (possessing) is used because the meaning is: "a group of gardens possessing delight," as one says: "the women went," and *al-bahja* is beauty, because the observer is delighted by it.

﴿Is there a god with God?﴾ Is He a rival who is joined to Him and made a partner to Him? It has been read as *ilhan maʿa Allah* (إلها مع الله), meaning: "Do you invoke [another god]?" or "Do you associate [others with Him]?" You may make both *hamzas* clear and place a prolonged vowel between them, and you may pronounce the second *hamza* as an intermediate sound (*bayn bayn*). ﴿They ascribe equals to Him﴾ means they make others equal to Him, or they turn away from the truth, which is the Oneness of God (*tawhid*).

"Amman ja'ala" and what follows it is a substitution (*badal*, in grammar, a replacement that takes the place of the original) for "amman khalaqa," so their ruling is the ruling of that clause. "Qararan" (a resting place): "dahaha wa sawwaha" (He spread it out and made it level), by settling upon it. "Hajizan" (a barrier), like His saying: "barzakhan" (a barrier).

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 27, verse 62:

Al-ḍarūrah (necessity): the condition that compels one to seek refuge. Al-iḍṭirār (compulsion) is its derived form (ifti'āl). One says: iḍṭarrahu ilā kadhā (he compelled him to such-and-such).

The doer and the object are both: muḍṭarr (one in compulsion). The muḍṭarr is the one whom illness, poverty, or one of the calamities of time has driven to seek refuge and to humble himself before God. It is reported from Ibn ʿAbbās, may God be pleased with them both, that it means one who is exhausted (al-majhūd). It is reported from al-Suddī that it means one who has no strength or power of his own. It has also been said: a sinner when he seeks forgiveness.

If you say: He has made the compelled (al-muḍṭarr) general by His saying ﴿He who answers the compelled one when he calls upon Him﴾, yet how many a compelled person calls upon Him and is not answered?

I say: the answering is contingent upon the thing asked for being a benefit (maṣlaḥah). For this reason, a servant's supplication is only fitting when it stipulates what is beneficial. As for al-muḍṭarr, it applies to the category absolutely; it is suitable for the whole of it and for a part of it. So there is no way to be certain of one of the two readings except by evidence. Evidence has been established for a part of it, namely the one whose request is answered by a benefit. Thus the general application is nullified.

﴿Caliphs of the earth﴾: successors in it. That is their inheriting its dwelling and their disposing of it, generation after generation. Or he intends by khilāfah sovereignty and dominion.

It is read yatadhakkarūn with the ya' and with assimilation (idghām), and with the ta' with assimilation and elision. Mā is superfluous (mazīdah), meaning: they remember with little remembrance. The meaning is negation of remembrance, and "little" is used to express negation.
He guides you by the stars in the sky and by the landmarks on the earth, when the night covers you while you travel on land and at sea.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 27, verse 64:

If it is asked: how was it said to them, ﴿Or who originates creation and then repeats it?﴾ while they deny the repetition (resurrection)? I answer:

Their excuse has been removed by enabling them to attain knowledge and acknowledgment, so no excuse remains for them in denial. ﴿Who sends down water from the sky and produces vegetation from the earth?﴾ ﴿If you are truthful﴾ that there is a god with Allah, then where is your proof for it?

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 27, verse 65:

If you say: Why is the name of Allah in the nominative, when Allah is exalted above being among those in the heavens and the earth? I answer:

It comes according to the dialect of the Banu Tamim, who say: "There is no one in the house except a donkey" (mā fī l-dār aḥad illā ḥimār), meaning: there is nothing in it except a donkey, as if no one had been mentioned. From this is his saying:

*ʿashiyyatu mā taghnā l-rimāḥu makānahā … wa-lā l-nabl illā l-mashrafī l-muṣammam*

[[al-nabl: Arab arrows. al-mashrafi: the sword, a nisba to the Masharif of Yemen. al-muṣammam: the one that is sharp and piercing through its hardness. It was the custom of combatants to shoot arrows when far apart; when they drew near they fought with spears, and when they met they struck with swords.

Mentioning the arrows after the spears is to dispel the assumption that the enemy was distant, as if the arrows were replacing the others. So the verse is a metonymy for the severity of the matter and the mingling of the two lines. The pronoun in makānahā refers to the war or to the swords. The exception after the negation is disjunctive (munqaṭiʿ), and its object must be in the accusative according to the Ḥijāzīs. It may be in the nominative, as here, according to the Tamīmīs: either as a substitute (badal), or on the assumption that the word excepted from is not mentioned and that the governing element is left free for what follows illā.]]

And their saying: "Zayd did not come to me except ʿAmr," and "Your brothers did not help him except his brothers." If you ask: What motivates choosing the Tamimi school over the Hijazi? I answer: a subtle secret motivated it [[The phrase "a subtle secret motivated it" is perhaps in the pattern faʿīla, meaning sharīfa. (ʿ)]]. It places the excepted term in the manner of his saying, "except the gazelles," after his saying, "there is no companion in it," so that the meaning comes to your saying: If Allah were among those in the heavens and the earth, then they would know the unseen. That is, their knowledge of the unseen is as impossible as Allah's being among them. Just as the meaning of what is in the verse [[The phrase "the meaning of what is in the verse" is the poet's saying: "A land with no companion in it, except the gazelles and the camels." (ʿ)]]: if the gazelles were companions, then there would be a companion in it, which contradicts the claim that it is empty of companions.

If you say: Why not hold that Allah is among those in the heavens and the earth, as the theologians say, "Allah is in every place," meaning that His knowledge is in all places, so that His essence is in them, so that you would not be forced into the Banu Tamim school? I answer: This is refused because His being in the heavens and the earth is figurative, while their being in them is literal, and it is not sound for a speaker to intend both the literal and the figurative with one expression. Moreover, your saying "those in the heavens and the earth," and your joining Him with them under one name, contains the appearance of equality, and such appearances must be removed from Him and from His attributes, exalted is He. Do you not see how the Prophet ﷺ said to the one who said, "Whoever disobeys them both has gone astray": "Evil is the orator of the people, you" [[Related by Muslim from the hadith of ʿAdī ibn Ḥātim.]]. And ʿĀʾisha, may Allah be pleased with her, said: "Whoever claims that he knows what will happen tomorrow has greatly slandered Allah" [[Agreed upon, from her narration within a longer hadith.]]. And Allah the Exalted says: "Say: None in the heavens and the earth knows the unseen except Allah" [Qur'an 27:65]. And one of them said: He concealed His unseen from creation and did not let anyone have knowledge of it, so that none of His servants would feel secure from His scheme. It was also said: it was revealed concerning the polytheists when they asked the Messenger of Allah ﷺ about the time of the Hour, *ayyāna* meaning "when." Had it been used as a name, it would be *fa'āl*, from *āna yaʾīnu*, and it would not take nunation. It is also read *īān*, with a kasra on the hamza.

The readings (qira'at, the recognised variant recitations of the Qur'an) include: "bal adraka," "bal idrāk," "bal idārak," "bal tadārak," "bal a'adraka" with two hamzas, "bal ā'adraka" with an alif between them, "bal adraka" with lightening and transfer of the vowel, and "bal iddaraka" with a fatha on the lām and a shadda on the dāl. Their origin is:

"bal a'addaraka?" as an interrogative (istifham). "Balā adraka." "Balā a'adraka." "Am tadārak." "Am adraka." These make twelve readings.

"Ida'ārak" originally was "tadārak," and the tā' was assimilated into the dāl (idghām, assimilation of consonants). "Iddaraka" is of the iftaʿala pattern.

The meaning of "adraka ʿilmuhum" is: their knowledge reached its end and was complete. "Iddaraka" means: it followed in succession and became firmly established. This has two aspects. The first: the causes of the firm establishment and completeness of knowledge, namely that the Resurrection is certainly coming, with no doubt in it, have come to them, and they were enabled to know it, yet they are doubtful and ignorant. This is His saying: ﴿بَلْ هُمْ فِي شَكٍّ مِنْهَا بَلْ هُمْ مِنْهَا عَمُونَ﴾. He means the polytheists among those in the heavens and the earth, because when they were part of the whole, their action was attributed to all, as one says: "The sons of so-and-so did such-and-such," when only some of them did it.

If you say: the verse was brought to single out God with knowledge of the unseen, and that the servants have no knowledge of any of it, and that the time of their resurrection and rising is among the unseen, of which they are unaware. How then does this meaning fit with describing the polytheists as denying resurrection, despite the firm establishment of the causes of knowledge and their ability to know?

I say: when it was mentioned that the servants do not know the unseen, nor are aware of the coming resurrection and its time, and this was an explanation of their inability and a description of the deficiency of their knowledge, it was joined to it that they have a greater incapacity than this, namely that they say of what must certainly occur, which is the time of the recompense for their deeds: "It will not happen," although they possess the causes of knowing its occurrence and the firm establishment of knowledge of it.

The second aspect: describing them with the firm establishment and completeness of knowledge is mockery of them, as you say to the most ignorant of people: "How knowledgeable you are!" as a jest. This is because they doubted and were blind to its affirmation, whose path to knowledge is well trodden, let alone that they would know the time of its occurrence, for which there is no path to knowledge.

In "adraka ʿilmuhum" and "adārak ʿilmuhum" there is another aspect: that "adraka" means "ended and perished," from your saying: "adraktu al-thamarah" (I reached the fruit, i.e., it ripened and was finished), because that is its final point, at which it ceases to exist. Al-Hasan, may God be pleased with him, explained it as "their knowledge was annihilated," and "tadārak" from "tadārak banū fulān" (the sons of so-and-so followed one another into destruction).

If you ask: what is the meaning of the reading of one who reads "bal a'adraka" as an interrogative? I say: it is an interrogative in the sense of denial of the attainment of their knowledge, and likewise the one who reads "am adraka" and "am tadārak," since "am" here means "bal" together with the hamza.

If you ask: what of the one who reads "balā adraka" and "balā a'adraka"? I say: when He brought "balā" after His saying ﴿وَمَا يَشْعُرُونَ﴾, its meaning was: "Yes, they are aware." Then He explained the awareness by His saying "adraka ʿilmuhum fī al-ākhirah" in the manner of mockery, whose meaning is emphasis in negating knowledge. It is as if He said: their awareness of the time of the Hereafter is that they do not know its occurrence, so it returns to negating awareness in the most emphatic form. As for the one who reads "balā a'adraka" as an interrogative, its meaning is: "Yes, they are aware of when they will be resurrected," then He denies their knowledge of its occurrence. When their knowledge of its occurrence is denied, no awareness of the time of its occurrence can be achieved for them, because knowledge of the time of an occurrence follows knowledge of the occurrence itself.

If you ask: what is the meaning of these three shifts (idrābāt, transitions of statement: bal)? I say: they are nothing but a depiction of their states. He described them first as not being aware of the time of resurrection, then as not knowing that the Resurrection is certainly coming, then as floundering in doubt and uncertainty, not removing it, though removal is possible. Do you not see that one who has not heard of the disagreement of schools of thought and their mutual misguidance is in a better state than one who has heard of it yet sits still, not directing his effort toward distinguishing truth from falsehood? Then consider one in worse condition, who is blind, or who is like an animal whose concern is absorbed in its belly and genitals, neither truth nor falsehood occurring to his mind, nor does he reflect on the outcome.

He made the Hereafter the source and origin of their blindness, so He followed it with "min" rather than "ʿan," because denial of the outcome and the recompense is what made them like cattle, not reflecting or perceiving.

The governing element (al-'amil) of ﴿idhā﴾ (when) is what indicates it, namely ﴿أَإِنَّا لَمُخْرَجُونَ﴾ (Are we indeed to be brought forth?), that is, the verb ﴿نخرج﴾ (nukhraj, "we shall be brought forth"). This is because before the governing of the active participle (ism al-fa'il) there stand obstacles [[His phrase "ism al-fa'il fīhi 'iqāban" may be a mistake for "ism al-maf'ūl," and "'iqāban" is the plural of "'uqba." Recorded by al-Ṣiḥāḥ. The wording of al-Nasafi is: "Because the active participle and the passive participle, after the interrogative hamza, or inna, or the lam of initiation, do not govern what precedes them, so how much more when these are combined." (ʿ)]], which are the interrogative hamza, inna, and the lam of initiation. One of them alone is sufficient, so how much more when they are combined?

The intended meaning is the bringing forth from the earth, or from the state of annihilation to life. Placing the interrogative particle before both ﴿idhā﴾ and ﴿inna﴾ together is denial upon denial, and rejection following rejection, and evidence of emphatic and exaggerated disbelief. The pronoun in ﴿innā﴾ refers to them and to their fathers, because their being dust has encompassed them and their fathers.

If you ask: this verse puts this (the bringing forth) before ﴿نَحْنُ وَآباؤُنا﴾ (naḥnu wa-ābāʾunā, "we and our fathers"), while in another verse ﴿نَحْنُ وَآباؤُنا﴾ is put before this. I answer: the fronting (taqdīm) is evidence that the fronted element is the purpose intentionally mentioned, and that the speech was driven for its sake. So in one of the two verses it shows that the resurrection (al-ba'th) is what the speech was specifically intended to address, and in the other it shows that the resurrected people (al-mab'ūth) are the focus in that context.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 27, verses 71–72:

They hastened the punishment that was promised. It was said to them: ﴿Perhaps some of what you seek to hasten has drawn close to you (radifa lakum)﴾, and this is the punishment of the Day of Badr. The lam was added for emphasis, like the ba' in ﴿and do not cast yourselves into destruction with your own hands﴾. Or the verb is taken to imply a verb that takes the lam, such as "danā lakum" (it drew near to you) and "azifa lakum" (it approached you). Its meaning is: it followed you and overtook you. It has been transitive with min, as in the saying:

"When we drew near to Umayr and his companions,
they turned and fled swiftly, and death was racing after them."

Radifa, meaning "followed", is transitive by itself, but here it has been given the sense of "drew near", so it takes min. A'naqa al-faras means the horse went at a swift, easy pace. Al-'Unuq is its verbal noun. The meaning is: when we drew near to Umayr and his companions for battle, they turned away in haste, while death was pressing after them from our side. He likened death to a lion on the path, in the form of the implicit metaphor (al-isti'ara al-makniyya, where only the comparand is mentioned), and attributed to it "neck" (al-'unuq) as an imaginative representation (takhyil), as though they had been pursued by the shooting of arrows. It is also permissible that he used death as a metaphor for himself and his people in the explicit form (al-tasrih), meaning: "and we were hastening after them". Mentioning the "neck" is then an abstraction (tajrid), because it suits the likened element.

That is: "we drew near to Umayr". Al-A'raj recited "radifa lakum" in the pattern of "dhahaba", and both are dialectal variants, though the kasra is more eloquent.

The words "asā" (perhaps), "la'alla" (perhaps) and "sawfa" (surely), when used in the promises and threats of kings, indicate the truth and seriousness of the matter, and that there is no room for doubt after them. They mean by this only to show their dignity and that they do not hasten to take vengeance, out of confidence in their domination and victory, and their certainty that their enemy will not escape them, and that a mere gesture toward their aims is sufficient on their part. In the same way proceeded the promise and threat of God.

Al-Fadl and al-fadilah: bestowal of favor (al-ifdal). One says "li-fulan fawadil fi qawmihi wa fudul," meaning he has favors and surplus bounties among his people.

The meaning is: He bestows favor upon them by delaying the punishment, and He does not hasten it upon them. Most of them do not recognize the due right of this blessing and do not give thanks for it, but out of their ignorance they seek to hasten the occurrence of the punishment. They are the Quraysh.

Some read "تكنّ" (tukinn). It is said: "kanantu al-shay'" and "akanntuhu," meaning: I concealed it and hid it. The meaning is: He knows what they conceal and what they disclose of enmity toward the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and their plotting against him, and He will requite them for that with what they deserve.

The thing that is hidden and concealed is called ghā'iba (hidden) and khāfiya (concealed), so the tā' in both is in the same position as in ʿāfiya (well-being) and ʿāqiba (outcome).

Their counterparts are naṭīḥa (the animal struck and killed by a blow), ramiyya (the animal shot by an arrow), and dhabīḥa (the slaughtered animal): in that they are nouns rather than adjectives. It is also permissible that both be adjectives, with the tā' serving for intensification, as in rāwiya in their saying: "Woe to the poet from the bad narration (riwāya al-sūʾ)," as if he had said: "There is nothing extremely hidden and concealed except that God knows it, encompasses it, and records it in the Preserved Tablet." Mubīn: clear and evident to whoever examines it among the angels.

They have differed concerning the Messiah, split into factions over him, and fallen into mutual denunciation over many matters, to the point that some of them cursed others. The Qur'an has come with a clarification of what they differed about, for them to adopt and submit to if they had been fair. He means the Jews and the Christians. ﴿For the believers﴾ means for whoever among them is fair and believes, i.e., from the Children of Israel, or from among them and others.

Is it not said, "Zayd strikes with his striking, and prevents with his preventing"? I say: its meaning is "by what He judges," namely His justice, for He only judges with justice; so He called the thing judged a "judgment" (hukm). Or He intended "by His wisdom" (bi-hikmatihi), and the reading of the one who read "bi-hukmihi" (with a short vowel) indicates this, the plural of hikmah (wisdom).

﴿And He is the Mighty﴾: so His judgment cannot be turned back. ﴿the Knowing﴾: of who is to be judged in his favour and who is to be judged against. Or: the Mighty in His retribution against the wrongdoers, the Knowing of the distinction between them and the righteous.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 27, verses 79–81:

He (Allah) commanded him (the Prophet) to rely upon Allah (tawakkul) and to pay little heed to the enemies of the religion. He gave as the reason for relying upon Allah that he stands upon the manifest truth (al-haqq al-ablaj), to which doubt and conjecture (zann) do not attach. In this there is an explanation that the possessor of the truth is deserving of trust in the handiwork of Allah and in His support,

and that one such as him is not forsaken. If you say: "Indeed you cannot make the dead hear" seems to be another reason for reliance (tawakkul); what is its aspect? I say: Its aspect is that the command to rely upon Allah was made a consequence of what used to vex the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) from the polytheists and the People of the Book: their abandonment of following him, and their accompanying that with harm and enmity. So it was fitting that the reliance of one such as him be justified by the fact that following them is a matter of which he has despaired, so nothing remains except seeking victory over them, given their hostility, and seeking sufficiency against their evils and harm. They were likened to the dead, though they were living with sound senses, because when they heard what was recited to them of the verses of Allah, they were like funnels of speech (aqmaa' al-qawl), their ears not comprehending it, and their hearing was no hearing. Their condition, given the absence of any benefit from hearing, was like the condition of the dead who have lost the faculty of hearing. Likewise is their likening to the deaf who are called to, yet do not hear. And they were likened to the blind, in that they lose the way, and no one can remove that from them, nor make them guides who see, except Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. If you say: what is the meaning of His words "when they turn their backs in retreat" (idha wallaw mudbirin)? I say: It is an emphasis on the state of the deaf, for when he distances himself from the caller by turning away from him in retreat, he is further from perceiving his voice. It was also read: "nor do you make the deaf hear, nor guide the blind" (wa-la yasma'u al-summu, wa-ma anta bi-hadi al-'umy), according to the original form, and "you guide the blind" (tahdi al-'umy). It is related from Ibn Mas'ud: "nor can you guide the blind" (wa-ma an tahdi al-'umy), and "guiding him away from error."

Like your saying: "He gave him to drink away from the craving (al-'aymah)" [the note of the editor: "al-'aymah" is the craving for milk, as in al-Sihah. (ʿ)], meaning: he removed him from it by giving drink, and removed him from error by guidance.

"Your hearing" (in tusmi'u) means: your making them hear is of no benefit except to those whom Allah knows believe in His signs, meaning: they affirm them as true; "so they are Muslims" (fa-hum muslimun), meaning: sincere, from His saying: "Yes, whoever submits his face to Allah" (bala man aslama wajhahu lillah), meaning: he made it wholly sound and sincere to Allah.

Zamakhshari's commentary (al-Kashshaf) on surah 27, verse 82:

The meaning and implication of the word (qawl) is named "the word" (al-qawl), namely what they were promised of the Hour's establishment and the punishment, and its occurrence: its coming about. The intended meaning is the approach of the Hour and the appearance of its portents, at a time when repentance will not benefit. The Beast of the earth (dabbat al-ard) is al-Jassasa. It is related in a hadith that its length is sixty cubits; no seeker can overtake it, and no fleeing one can escape it. [[Al-Tha'labi related it from the hadith of Hudhayfa, without his saying "and she is al-Jassasa"; part of it will come in al-Hakim and others in the following narration.]]

It is also related: it has four legs, down and feathers, and two wings. And from Ibn Jurayj in its description: the head of an ox, the eye of a pig, the ear of an elephant, the horn of a camel, the neck of an ostrich, the chest of a lion, the colour of a leopard, the flank of a cat, the tail of a ram, and the hoof of a camel. And the distance between its two joints is twelve cubits by the cubit of Adam, upon him be peace.

It is also related: it will not emerge except its head, and its head reaches the sky's expanses (a'nan al-sama'), or reaches the clouds. [[His saying "its head reaches the sky's expanses" – in al-Sihah, "a'nan al-sama'" means its plates and what projects from its horizons, as if it were the plural of "a'nan". The common people say "anan al-sama'".]] And from Abu Hurayra: in it is every colour, and the distance between its two horns is a farsakh for a rider. And from al-Hasan, may Allah be pleased with him: its emergence is not complete until after three days. And from Ali, may Allah be pleased with him: that it emerges for three days while people look on, and only a third of it emerges. And from the Prophet ﷺ: he was asked, "From where will the beast emerge?" He said, "From the most sacred of the mosques in the sight of Allah [[Al-Tabari related it through Rab'i from Hudhayfa ibn al-Yaman: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ mentioned the beast, and I said, 'O Messenger of Allah, from where will it emerge?' Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 27, verse 83:

﴿فَهُمْ يُوزَعُونَ﴾ means: their first is held back until their last, so that they gather together and are then thrown headlong into the Fire. This is an expression for the great number and the spread of its extremities, just as the soldiers of Sulayman were described with it. Likewise His saying ﴿فَوْجاً﴾ (fawjan, "a host"), for the fawj (company) is a large group. From the same root is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿يَدْخُلُونَ فِي دِينِ اللَّهِ أَفْواجاً﴾ ("They enter the religion of Allah in companies").

It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both: Abu Jahl, al-Walid ibn al-Mughira, and Shayba ibn Rabi'a are driven before the people of Makkah, and likewise the leaders of all the nations will be gathered before their peoples toward the Fire.

If you say: what is the difference between the first "min" (مِنْ) and the second? I say: the first is for partitive meaning (li-l-tab'id), and the second is for explanation (li-l-tabyin), like His saying ﴿مِنَ الْأَوْثانِ﴾ ("of the idols").

The **wāw** here is for the **ḥāl** (circumstantial clause, ḥāl), as if he said: "Did you deny them at first glance, without reflection or consideration that would lead to full knowledge of their reality, and of whether they deserve belief or denial?" Or it is for **ʿaṭf** (conjunction, ʿaṭf), meaning: "You denied them, and along with your denial you did not apply your minds to verify and examine them. The recipient of a letter may deny that it came from its writer, yet still not refrain from reading it, understanding its contents, and grasping its meanings."

﴿Then what were you doing?﴾ is said for rebuke alone. They did nothing but deny, so they cannot say, "We have believed in them," since there was only belief in them or denial of them.

An example: you say to your shepherd, whom you know to be a bad, petty shepherd, "Are you eating my camels (niʿam), or what are you doing with them?" You make the thing you begin with, and make it the basis and foundation of your speech, the fact you know of his eating and corruption. You throw in your words, "or what are you doing with them?", although you know that he does nothing with them but eat, in order to confound him ("li-tabhatahu": his saying "to confound him" means to dumbfound and bewilder him (ع)), and to let him know that you are aware that nothing will come from him except eating them, and that he cannot claim to guard and reform them, given what is known of the opposite.

Or the meaning is: "Did you have no works in the world except disbelief and denial of God's signs? Or what else were you doing besides that?" That is, they had no other work. It is as if they were created only for disbelief and disobedience, whereas they were created for faith and obedience. They are addressed with this before they are thrown on their faces into the Fire, and then they are thrown into it. This is His saying: ﴿And the word will fall upon them﴾, meaning that the promised punishment will overwhelm them because of their wrongdoing, which is denial of God's signs. It will preoccupy them from speaking and making excuses, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿This is a day when they will not speak﴾.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 27, verse 87:

If you ask: why is it said "fa-faza'a" (so he was terrified) rather than "fa-yafza'" (so he will be terrified)? I answer: for a subtle point, which is to indicate the certainty and establishment of the terror, that it is bound to occur and will surely befall those in the heavens and the earth, because the past tense verb indicates that the action has occurred and is considered certain. The intended meaning is their terror at the first blast, when they will swoon, ﴿except whom God wills﴾: except those whose hearts God has made firm among the angels. They said: they are Jibril, Mika'il, Israfil, and the Angel of Death, peace be upon them. It was also said: the martyrs. And from al-Dahhak: the houris, the guardians of the Fire, and the bearers of the Throne. And from Jabir: Musa (peace be upon him) is among them, because he swooned once. A similar statement is God's words: ﴿And the Trumpet will be blown, and whoever is in the heavens and whoever is on the earth will swoon, except whom God wills﴾.

It has been read: "atawhu" and "ataahu", and "dakhirin". The plural is according to the meaning, and the singular according to the wording. Al-dakhir and al-dakhr: the humbled, the abased. It was also said: "coming" means their presence at the place of standing after the second blast. It is also permissible that it means their return to His command and their submission to Him.

And you see the mountains and think them fixed, but they pass by as the clouds pass by. ﴿The handiwork of God, who perfected everything﴾. The meaning is: "jamidah" is from "jamada" (to remain still in its place) when it does not move. The mountains gather and move as the wind moves the clouds. When an observer looks at them, he supposes them to be standing still in one place, while they are passing swiftly, as clouds pass. So too with great, numerous bodies: when they move, their motion can hardly be discerned, as al-Nabigha said describing an army:

*With a host like a mountain, you would think them*
*Standing still for the pilgrims, while the riding-beasts trot briskly.*

[[Of al-Nabigha. "Al-arman" means a high mountain, and "al-tawd" a great mountain. He used "al-arman" as a metaphor for the army, then compared it to "al-tawd" to convey exaggeration in its numbers. "Al-hajj" is a collective noun whose singular is "hajjah". "Al-rikab" means mounts, having no singular from its own form. "Al-hamlajah" means a gentle, easy pace; it is Persian, Arabicised. "Al-hamlaj" means swift. He says: we fought the enemy with a mighty army, you would think them standing still for a purpose because of their numbers, while in fact their mounts are hastening their pace.]]

"Ṣun'a Allah" (the handiwork of God) is an emphatic verbal noun (maṣdar mu'akkad), like His saying ﴿God has promised﴾ and ﴿the dye of God﴾. But the emphatic verbal noun is elided, and it is the governing verb of "the day the Trumpet is blown". The meaning is: "And on the day the Trumpet is blown, and such-and-such occurs, God rewards the good-doers and punishes the wrongdoers." Then He said, "the handiwork of God", meaning the rewarding and the punishing. He made this handiwork among the things He has perfected and brought about with wisdom and rightness, when He said: ﴿The handiwork of God, who perfected everything﴾. That is to say, His recompensing good with reward and evil with punishment is part of His firm ordering of things and perfecting of them, and of His running them according to the requirements of wisdom: He knows what the servants do and what they deserve from Him, and so He repays them according to that. Then He summarised this with His saying: ﴿Whoever comes with a good deed, for him is better than it; and they, from the terror of that day, will be safe. And whoever comes with an evil deed, their faces will be thrown into the Fire. Are you recompensed except for what you used to do?﴾ So consider the eloquence of this speech, the beauty of its composition and arrangement, the aptness of its "idmād" (binding, i.e. its tight linking), the firmness of its exposition, [[His saying "its aptness of idmād and firmness of tafsīr": in al-Ṣiḥāḥ, "ḍamada al-jurḥ, yaḍmuduhu, ḍamadan" means he bound the wound with a bandage. And "al-raṣīn" means the firm, established. "Raṣuna", with a ḍamma, "raṣānah". (ʿ)]] and how its parts hold to one another, as if it were poured in one single casting. Something of this kind has overwhelmed the powers and silenced the tongues. When such a verbal noun comes after a statement, it comes as a witness to its truth and an announcer of its soundness, and that it could not have been other than what it is.

Do you not see His saying: ﴿the handiwork of God﴾, ﴿the dye of God﴾, ﴿the promise of God﴾, ﴿the nature of God﴾ — after He marked them by attributing them to Himself with the mark of exaltation, how He followed them with His saying: ﴿who perfected everything﴾, ﴿And who is better than God in dye?﴾, ﴿God does not fail His promise﴾, ﴿There is no altering of the creation of God﴾. It was read "taf'alūn" (you do) with the second-person form. ﴿Then for him is better than it﴾: it means multiplication, and that the deed comes to an end while the reward endures; and how far apart are the deed of the servant and the deed of the Master! It was said: ﴿for him is better than it﴾ means: for him is a good that arises from it, and that is Paradise. It is reported from Ibn ʿAbbās that "the good deed" is the word of testimony.

It was read "yawma'idhin" (that day) with a fatḥa and with the genitive construction, because it is added to something not fully declinable; and it was read in the accusative with tanwīn on "faza'" (terror). If you ask: what is the difference between the two terrors? I say: the first terror is that which no one is free from upon perceiving a severe event that strikes suddenly, of fright and awe, even if the one who does good is safe from harm reaching him, just as a man enters upon a king with a fearful breast and a trembling heart, even if it is an hour of honour, of generosity, of kindness and of appointment. [[His saying "and a trembling heart (qalb wajib)": in al-Ṣiḥāḥ, "wajaba al-qalb, wajīban" means it throbbed. (ʿ)]]

As for the second, it is the fear of punishment. If you ask: what is the meaning of the one who reads "min faza'" with tanwīn? I say: it may bear two meanings. As for what befalls a person of dread and awe at the great terrors and horrors he sees, none is free from it, because human nature requires it, and reports and traditions indicate it. It may be that the mention of "faces" is a notice that they will be thrown upon their faces therein, upside down. ﴿Are you recompensed?﴾ In it, the shift of person (iltifāt) is permissible, and the relating of what is said to them at the time of their being thrown is by the implicit supposition of a "saying".

I say: the first terror is that which no one is free from upon perceiving a severe event that strikes suddenly, of fright and awe, even if the one who does good is safe from harm reaching him, just as a man enters upon a king with a fearful breast and a trembling heart, even if it is an hour of honour, of generosity, of kindness and of appointment. [[His saying "and a trembling heart (qalb wajib)": in al-Ṣiḥāḥ, "wajaba al-qalb, wajīban" means it throbbed. (ʿ)]]

As for the second, it is the fear of punishment. If you ask: what is the meaning of the one who reads "min faza'" with tanwīn? I say: it may bear two meanings. "From a single terror": which is fear of punishment. As for what befalls a person of dread and awe at the great terrors and horrors he sees, none is free from it, because human nature requires it, and reports and traditions indicate it. And "from a terror, a severe one, most extreme in its severity, which description cannot grasp": and that is the fear of the Fire. "Amina" is transitive by means of a preposition and directly, as in His saying: ﴿Do they then feel safe from the plan of God?﴾. It was said: the evil deed is associating partners with God. The whole is expressed by the face, the head and the neck, so it is as if it were said: "they were thrown into the Fire", as in His saying: ﴿So they were thrown into it﴾. It may be that the mention of "faces" is a notice that they will be thrown upon their faces therein, upside down. ﴿Are you recompensed?﴾ In it, the shift of person (iltifāt) is permissible, and the relating of what is said to them at the time of their being thrown is by the implicit supposition of a "saying".
